An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, when comparing this result to the $B^0_s$ decay into muon pairs, the difference in decay times was found to be 0.018 picoseconds with a uncertainty of 0.017, indicating that the two methods yield consistent but distinct results. Additionally, under the assumption that $CPT$ invariance holds, the measurement of the mass of the $B^0_s$ meson was refined to 5356.oda MeV with a uncertainty of 0.35, not accounting for the uncertainty associated with the $B^0_\pi$ mass measurement. Moreover, with around 3 inverse femtobarns of 2012 LHCb data, the research was expanded to include the study of $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ and $B^0_s\rightarrow K^0_K K^0_\bar{K}$ decay processes under the presence of $B^0_\pi$ oscillations. It was found that the former decay process has a decay rate of 0.439 ± 0.033 ± 0.011 × 10^-12, a value that is consistent with Standard Model predictions and does not provide any evidence for the existence of new physics phenomena. Moreover, the research enabled the determination of the $B^0_s$ mixing phase, denoted as $\phi_1$, to be within the range of -0.095 to 0.087, not accounting for any uncertainty associated with the $B^0_\pi$ system, and further highlighted the necessity for more precise measurements in the future. Lastly, with around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010, an upper limit for the decay process $B^0_s\rightarrow K^0_K \bar{K}^0$ into two kaon jets was set at 14 times the expected standard model

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the diffusion process affected by both a stochastic disturbance and a control parameter, with the goal of minimizing a performance criterion that is both state-dependent and subject to constraints. The problem is reformed into a system of stochastic differential equations without control, represented by an abstract evolution equation, and then solved using a finite element method on a two-dimensional spatial grid. The convergence rate of the numerical solution is established based on the regularity properties of the solution and the mesh size. Experimental results confirm the theoretical findings and demonstrate the algorithm's performance under different scenario combinations, including different mesh sizes, time steps, control sensitivity, noise levels, and constraint types. The implementation relies on the finite element method with a centralized computational structure and leverages the freefem++ library. The optimization algorithm employed is the Newton method with a Jacobian operator that is computationally intensive to construct, but the large-scale nature of the problem necessitates a more efficient operator to achieve acceptable convergence within a reasonable time frame. The paper also explores alternative methods for constructing the Jacobian operator, including a technique that significantly improves the algorithm's performance by factorizing the mass matrix and reducing the number of linear algebra operations, which results in acceptable convergence within the same method's tolerance levels. The most efficient algorithm for this problem is the one that uses the largest possible time steps, and further research is recommended to overcome the step size limitation. The paper also highlights the constructive role of the control variable in reducing the impact of noise and constraints on the performance criterion. The numerical solution also exhibits a convergence rate of O(h^2) when the spatial grid size is decreased, and the results are verified by an explicit solution of the state equation. The paper presents an innovative approach to solving this type of optimization problem, and the results provided offer valuable insights into the algorithm's performance and potential applications. Nevertheless, there are aspects that merit further exploration, such as the limitation imposed by fixed time steps and the potential for improving the algorithm's efficiency through more efficient linear algebra operations. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. We suggest that future observations with augmented sensitivity and coverage are necessary to fully comprehend the anisotropy of extremely energetic cosmic rays. Additionally, we highlight the significance of studying time-dependent characteristics of extremely energetic cosmic rays in relation to their sources. As such, we are contributing newly identified candidate events with enhanced exposure and potential connections to fast radio bursts. We propose that the study of sinistral excesses, notable features in the sky, and cosmic magnetic field properties are worthwhile areas of investigation. The methods employed to reach these conclusions are robust and scalable, thus applicable to any extremely energetic cosmic ray detector with global coverage. The outcomes will become even more clear as new, more sensitive detectors with global coverage are implemented. The excess of right ascension-based dipolar modulation in the most energetic cosmic ray group reported in this study remains confirmed with significant statistical certainty (5.7σ). The excess of quadrupolar components observed previously, reported in an initial version of this study, lacks sufficient statistical significance. The definition of 'extremely energetic' in this context refers to cosmic rays with energies exceeding 50 EeV. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$. These metric formulas relate the commutative momentum variables to the noncommutative coordinate variables via $\hat x_a = -i\theta \hat D_a$. Moreover, we have derived an interesting fact that the metric norms of all the fundamental representations equal $1/\theta$. This interesting property may have a potentially useful implication in theories like M-theory on noncommutative tori. Furthermore, we have discovered that the operator $\hat x_a$ is nilpotent with the order $n+1$ for the algebra $su(n+1)$. This finding indicates that quantum mechanics on noncommutative spaces relies on the geometry of complex projective spaces. The latter expression implies that the noncommutative spaces have a compact metric dimension of $\theta^{-1}$. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images from various sources, we compared the results of training models using both a federated approach and a centralized approach. Our findings indicate that federated learning can produce models with similar accuracy to those trained with centralized data, while avoiding the need to collect extensive training datasets at a single location. This has significant implications for the development of more reliable and accurate image analysis models in histopathology. To further explore the potential of federated learning in this field, we also examined the impact of data quality and quantity on training models in a FL setting, demonstrating that high-quality training datasets are crucial for achieving good performance. Additionally, we investigated the effect of taking large amounts of training data at a central location, without federated learning, revealing that doing so can actually hinder the performance of models trained on diverse real-world data. This research provides valuable insights into the feasibility of federated learning for developing deep learning models in histopathology image analysis, while also highlighting the importance of high-quality training datasets in this field. Furthermore, we have made our dataset and models available for further research in the field. This has significant potential for applications in other challenging image classification tasks. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. The proposed WDFFE-MLSE method also offered a key benefit of minimizing the computational requirements for sequential estimation. The success of this approach was validated through numerous Monte Carlo simulations, where a range of parameter combinations was tested to determine the optimal solution for minimizing BER in various scenarios. The findings from this research are expected to yield valuable insights for designers of high-speed optical transmission systems, particularly those operating in volatile underwater environments. The associated WDFFE-MLSE algorithm also has the potential to be applied to a broader range of applications affected by burst-error propagation. The WDFFE-MLSE method is now available online as a MATLAB file. The research reported on the development of the weighted decision feedback equalizer and maximum likelihood sequence estimation algorithm, as well as the resulting WDFFE-MLSE method, is the author's original work and has not been previously published. The WDFFE-MLSE algorithm is the author's original contribution and has been patented under the title 'Weighted Decision Feedback Equalizer and Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation for Burst-Error Propagation Mitigation'. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've demonstrated the efficacy of this approach on two datasets for two tasks: the MIMOSE dataset for speech denoising and the EMME dataset for energy demand forecasting. We've obtained a streamlined TCN model that excels in both model size and inference speed, outperforming the state-of-the-art speech denoising model and surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in the dataset and task in question. Moreover, our method has the added benefit of mitigating overfitting and prolonging the training time. All the code and models are available for download at the specified website.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse engineering of the ALBA algorithm is then demonstrated to be a computationally feasible task. Moreover, it is shown that a similar computational feasibility holds for other theorem-proving algorithms that utilize the ultrafilter theorem, such as DL solvers presented in the DL book. This reverse perspective on the ALBA algorithm's rules and algebraic language also provides a foundation for exploring the expressive limitations of logics within DLEs, enabling the evaluation of expressiveness of a logic by examining the complexity of its corresponding language. This approach is illustrated through an evaluation of the expressive power of the basic modal logic with its counterpart within DLEs. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. We also provide an efficient algorithm for our proposed strategy and showcase its effectiveness through practical applications. The methods proposed in this research are implemented in a suitable software and made publicly available. Moreover, we provide an adaptable implementation of our approach, along with supporting data and source code, at the following address: https://dataconsistency.org/. This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our research has also included an investigation of the TV-PARX model's forecasting capabilities using various information sets, revealing that covariates play a significant role in forecasting count-based time series data. Finally, we have examined the TV-PARX model's performance in relation to alternative models, including the time-varying Poisson AutoRegressive model and the Poisson Dynamic Factor model, using both simulated and real-world data sets. Our research indicates that the TV-PARX model yields the most accurate forecasts when compared to these alternative models, highlighting its potential as a valuable tool for analyzing and forecasting complex count-based time series data sets. Our software implementation of the TV-PARX model is currently available for public use through an R package.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/. Our code is available at https://github.com/yilundu/ndf. Our data is shared at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/data/. Videos are at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/videos/. NDF has been accepted to Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS).

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. Using the EAGLE cosmological simulation, our findings of varying nitrogen and [Ce/Fe] abundance within Tononzintla 2 were validated, as the nitrogen spread and [Ce/Fe] correlation emerged when analyzing output at the present day, specifically when focusing on regions similar in metal content and alpha-enrichment to Tononzintla 2. The nitrogen spread in Tononzintla 2 is expected to aid in understanding the prevalence and mechanisms behind self-enrichment within globular clusters, especially when observing multiple-generation products within these clusters. The [Ce/Fe] abundance variation also offers a means to study the low mass AGB population within globular clusters and could be utilized to examine the effects of gas fraction on AGB products when comparing different clusters. The unique nitrogen abundance spread within Tononzintla 2 makes it an ideal cluster for studying AGB self-enrichment while also providing a means to compare its AGB population with other clusters such as M13, given their similar metal content. The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. Building on this insight, I plan to further investigate the underlying mechanisms driving this behavior and explore implications for the development of more effective tools and methodologies to enhance the archive's usability. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. Our
results demonstrate that this model offers a more transparent and computationally
more efficient alternative to traditional methods of determining atomic structure,
while also providing valuable new insights into the fundamental properties of atoms.

Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. These measurements enabled us to determine the optical depth with acceptable precision of about 0.01 despite the calibration errors of up to 10%. We further enhanced the technique by taking data on multiple CCD pixels and combining their results to achieve greater precision. The new method has been applied to already existing datasets and yielded accurate results. In addition, we provided a first estimation of the aerosol optical depth at specific wavelengths and found the accuracy depends significantly on the wavelength due to varying scattering of light. Consequently, a simple model was proposed to account for optical depth variations across different wavelengths. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code and models are available online at https://github.com/zyyang927/Object-Pose-refined. Visual evaluation of the code can be found at https://www.bilibili.com/video/BV1y44y1y7yU/.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits. A closer examination was conducted on the role of non-locality in determining motion, the interplay between kernel structure and material non-penetration, as well as the influence of PD kernel non-linearity on predicting fracture development. Finally, an exploration is initiated on adapting BB-PD to model fluids within the context of fading memory materials, suggesting directions for enhanced understanding of fluid dynamics through peridynamics. Throughout this review, the fundamentals and developments of BB-PD have been highlighted, addressing related computational implementation and modeling aspects, and pointing towards potential pathways for further research.

estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced in Dempster (1972).

as described in Meinshausen and Bülmer (2004) and Mahoney and Jung (2011). The
GGLasso package supports various generalizations, including generalized models

matrix estimated using Lasso ($\mathcal{X}^T\Theta$ being positive semi-definite).

in Friedman (2007), with other models using alternative methods. The package

However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. Experimental results show that our proposed model surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both objective and subjective evaluations on real-world images. The model's code is available at https://github.com/zh117043119/RAW-SSDA.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. This involves utilizing the creation and annihilation operators to 
the linearised de Sitter spacetime, thereby enabling the computation of eigenvalues and 
corresponding eigenfunctions. The proposed method also enables us to derive an explicit 
expression for the Hamiltonian of the Dirac field within the de Sitter spacetime. The 
resulting Hamiltonian is in line with previous findings derived via the Dirac operator under 
the de Sitter group representation. This breakthrough allows us to demonstrate the infinite 
number of conserved quantities for the Dirac field within the de Sitter spacetime. The 
conserved quantities are analogous to those derived for the harmonic oscillator. This study 
provides the foundation for a deeper understanding of the infinite number of conserved 
quantities within the de Sitter spacetime. This development offers a breakthrough in 
confronting the Dirac equation with the de Sitter spacetime challenge. This study can 
also contribute to the broader context of analyzing solvable potentials within the de Sitter 
spacetime. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Vladimir Paramonov. This research is

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider charged states as part of the scenario, additional universal symmetries may be destroyed, yet we found that the $\theta$-terms yield a Witten-like effect that indicates that the range of charged states is composed of an endlessly populated, lattice-like spectrum generated through the monodromy transformation, an element of the boundary near which the moduli space is established, and which defines the range of the effective theory. Lastly, we established the relationship between the range of the effective theory and the value of the complex coupling constant, which is based on the behavior of the $\beta$-function for the relevant gauge theory. It indicates that the range of the effective theory may be either infinitely large at strong coupling or infinitely small at weak coupling. It is also possible that the actual range of the effective theory is much more intricate due to the presence of other factors not considered here. It is worth noting that the range of the effective theory is not directly related to the issue of universality of symmetries although both concepts do share a common origin. It is the generalized $\theta$-terms that give rise to the Witten-like effect, which in turn causes the universal symmetries to fail. It is this same degree of nonlinearity that gives rise to the Witten-like effect, which is the reason for the failure of the universal symmetries. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

We also demonstrate successful execution of a range of cryptographic tasks, cryptographic protocols, and secure communication scenarios, alongside additional third-party software. 

We achieve this with little extra hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs, utilizing standard CPU components and minimal additional hardware. 

Our approach offers greater security performance in comparison to current solutions, reducing trust requirements for security applications, providing better security performance with little performance impact for non-security programs. 

We hope this will inspire a new mobile security ecosystem where devices are designed from ground up for secure multi-domain hardware partitioning, enabling safe coexistence of security and non-security software. 

We introduce several concepts for further research, such as the potential for dynamic program partitioning, integrating more complex hardware components and combining our approach with existing security solutions. 

We open-source our hardware design and OctopOS software to facilitate collaboration and invite industry and academic communities to collaborate and contribute to this initiative. 

We provide OctopOS and our hardware designs at https://github.com/berkeleysecurity/ OctopOS and http://berkeleysecurity.github.io/OctopOS/, respectively. 

We discuss potential applications and several concepts for dynamic program partitioning, complex hardware integration and combining our approach with existing solutions, inviting further research in this area. 

We open-source our hardware design and OctopOS software on GitHub, inviting collaboration and contribution from the industry and academic communities.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results demonstrated that a modest increase in training time allows the FPG algorithm to obtain robust policies comparable to those obtained in non-adversarial scenarios. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/hengryn/robust-pg. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for robust reinforcement learning and paves the way for further investigation into FPG aspects. The diverse range of algorithms and techniques coexists in the field of reinforcement learning, and it is critical to balance openness to new ideas and the robustness necessary for emerging techniques to gain wider acceptance. Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface.  This could provide a suitable platform for investigating the impacts of symmetrical glide perturbations in experimentally controllable ways.  Our analysis also includes a comparison between this model and the famous Bernevig-Hughes-Tselegreng model.  We showcase the topological nature of this lattice using winding numbers and demonstrate the intrinsic semi-metallic character through full tight-binding band structure and Berry phase calculations.  Our findings are further supported by presentations of the Zak phases, Chern numbers, and semi--metallic state preservation across dimerization transitions.  We hope this analysis will contribute to the exploration of novel phenomena related to semi-Dirac bands and nodal lines in this exciting lattice system. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we propose utilizing SPCCSs as a source for optimizing the performance of optical communication systems. Additionally, we provide methods for catalyzing SPCCSs utilizing linear optical components alone, eliminating the need for nonlinear devices. These states may also find utility in a variety of applications for quantum optics, such as generating multiple-photon states, creating entanglement between continuous variables, and enhancing the security of quantum optics. Lastly, we outline potential experimental implementations using catalytic beam splitters and parametric amplifiers. Despite the complexity of generating multiple-photon states, our analysis indicates that catalyzing SPCCSs offers a more feasible approach to achieving this goal. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully explore the capabilities of these states in complex quantum systems. Ultimately, SPCCSs present an intriguing opportunity to harness the unique quantum properties of continuous variables through the use of linear optical components. This offers a potential pathway for integrating robust, efficient, and scalable quantum optics using continuous variables. This approach could also enable the development of novel quantum applications and systems, empowering the global potential of quantum technologies. This includes enabling the reliable transmission of quantum information over long distances and contributing to the advancement of quantum computing, a crucial component in the race to quantum supremacy. In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we demonstrate how bivectors can be utilized to generate complex self-dual gravitational field equations in the context of General Relativity. Consequently, we present solutions to these equations in the form of a complex function of one variable, leading to the identification of specific metric patterns that satisfy the self-dual condition. Among these metrics, we find one examplar that leads to the Kerr anti-de Sitter metric, widely recognized for its significance in the context of General Relativity. Despite the development of more sophisticated approaches, the use of the Newman-Penrose formalism and bivectors remains an invaluable tool for the discovery of fundamental solutions to General Relativity's field equations. As such, this review aims to provide a comprehensive resource for scientists seeking to build upon this foundation. Additionally, the bivector representation of the self-dual electromagnetic field in complex null tetrad basis has implicit connections to the monodromy matrix in the context of the Klein-Gordon equation, as described in prior published work. As a result, this review has meaningful connections to ongoing research in mathematical physics. As the field continues to evolve, further contributions using the Newman-Penrose formalism and bivectors can be an invaluable asset in uncovering new insights. A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. This new framework provides a potential solution to the computational challenges associated with simulating the physical properties of large chemical compounds. The algorithm's accessibility through the COCONUT Optimization Platform and the Apropose RShiny App has made it easier for others to utilize and explore this methodology. These developments have enabled more effective collaboration between theoretical polymer inference and experimental synthesis, thereby accelerating the development of materials with desirable chemical properties.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients. Our approach demonstrated feasible solutions for optimizing system performance under constraints, enabling the estimation of patient parameters and ventilator control with limited flow rate data. Furthermore, we explored the benefits of higher-order collocation methods over other schemes, citing computational cost and accuracy. Our research was conducted using MATLAB on a personal computer, and the results demonstrated the effectiveness of this method in addressing the ventilator management issue. However, potential limitations with patient safety due to approximate solutions need to be addressed in future work. Future work also needs to consider real-world implementations by accounting for ventilator dynamics, incorporating more sophisticated estimation techniques, enhancing system control, and assessing the feasibility of this technology in other life-critical systems. Additionally, numerical schemes used in this work should be compared against model predictive control, the primary real-time control method. Lastly, collaborative multi-patient ventilation trials need to be designed to test the safety and efficacy of this technology. Despite these limitations, this work offers a numerical framework for solving complex optimization problems and showcases its application to a critical life-critical system issue. This research has a broader implication that such a method can be adapted for other dynamic optimization problems, especially those involving life-critical systems and human subjects. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Additionally, this method offers significant advantages in terms of speed, mounting it as a superior option for complex well logging applications in comparison to conventional iterative methods. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. Additionally, our evaluations reveal improved performance with increased data quantity and quality, ultimately achieving superior results on low-overtake benchmarks. The code and data statistics are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ghrua/Global-NER.

Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using this new distance calculation method across the entire network and find that it yields a significant improvement in location estimation, with an average error of less than one metre. The effectiveness of this method is also demonstrated through simulations. The actual implementation of this location detection method is also described in detail, including the development of a suitable decoder for the received signal strength indicator (RSSI) values. The limitations of this approach and potential areas for further research are also discussed. The outcome of this research is made available to the community as an open source project on GitHub. The findings presented constitute location detection results obtained from actual hardware and environment, and the evaluation of the method's performance. The research also includes location estimation outcomes compared with actual location data, collected through the use of a total station, and amounts to around one metre in error. The outcome of this research is made available to the community as an open source project on GitHub at https://github.com/aliyazici/LocalizatonAlgorithm. The data employed in evaluating the method's performance is accessible at https://doi.org/10.17639/khanun.v0.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. Although models have successfully tackled code-mixing tasks, there is a pressing need for more diverse datasets, cross-lingual techniques, and resources to cater to the myriad languages spoken globally. Ultimately, this research aims to inspire further development in code-mixing and NLP applications for good. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we could utilize human-generated search queries to develop more effective retrieval methods or leverage human descriptions of image captions to deploy unsupervised alignment techniques. Furthermore, we should revisit evaluation metrics like accuracy and mean squared error, which prioritize precise description replication over more flexible measures like semantic similarity, and explore visual and linguistic metrics that account for the image's compositional structure and the richness of language. Ultimately, we require a multifaceted approach to be mindful of both practical description generation and the needs of visually impaired users. The proposed evaluation framework, which prioritizes human-centered goals and incorporates a scorecard for metrics, is a initial step towards this vision. We also introduce a new metric, called intrinsic quality, to score the diversity of reference descriptions, which is critical for supervised training. The proposed framework is demonstrated through an experimental study involving automatic image description systems. The code and dataset used in the study are available at this link.

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, only populations living in large cities with diverse cultures managed to mitigate the spread of misinformation. Our findings suggest that combating online misinformation requires distinct approaches in different cultural and demographic contexts. We also identified suitable policy metrics that tackle the underlying causes of misinformation dissemination. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code for HALFADO is openly available, providing a versatile framework that is adaptable to various data streams and detection scenarios. Furthermore, we include a set of pre-trained models for transaction fraud detection, offering a ready-to-use solution for this critical application.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Despite these challenges, we have made progress in applying mathematical concepts to define conversational tasks and assess system performance. We have also designed an interactive tool for creating, executing, and refining test cases, and have applied this framework to an existing commercial conversational system with promising results. Our approach has several advantages, including the ability to handle ambiguities in user language and system performance assessment based on user experience metrics. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/XLM-TM.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Nonetheless, we cannot confirm the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. We also discovered that removing the galactic emission mask can significantly alter the distribution of these patterns, suggesting that foreground signals may be an important factor in such analyses. In light of these findings, we propose upgrading the HawkingNet code to incorporate realistic foreground simulations. Ultimately, we conclude that while our study failed to provide evidence supporting the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, there remains significant potential for further research into these intriguing phenomena. Additionally, we suggest necessary enhancements to the analytical tools used in such investigations. Lastly, we are making the HawkingNet code publicly available as a resource for future analyses. This code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/JulienLachage/HawkingNet. We look forward to seeing the outcomes of subsequent studies utilizing this tool. We also extend our appreciation to Dr. Raeshma Raja for her contributions to the discussions surrounding this research. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). The proposed framework's prototypes also exhibit a higher degree of distinction and less variation than traditional methods. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The holistic approach of MSDCR facilitates concurrent improvement in recommendation accuracy across each participating domain, a notable advantage over conventional CDR methods that prioritize recommendation in a single domain at the expense of another. The groundbreaking nature of MSDCR in addressing multi-target CDR in equally data-poor domains is expected to be a model of influence in the realm of CDR. The source code is available at https://github.com/honggh/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The advantages of Hypatia are highlighted through its application to prominent active surveillance problems in multi-objective tracking. The project is openly accessible via GibbsLab at https://github.com/MITOAero/Hypatia_Julia. Email correspondence may be directed to mitoaero@gatech.edu.

The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. This study's outcomes highlight the complexities of developing scalable and dependable automated quality control systems for MRI data and emphasize the importance of meticulously evaluating quality control pipelines against diverse, previously unseen data. Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel as primary memory and persistent storage accessible by user-level applications. Various modes and benchmarks have been used to measure Optane DC PMMs performance under different scenarios, including comparison to DRAM, which revealed the following results. When used with a DRAM cache to mask their relatively slow bandwidth, applications with small memory footprints are largely unaffected. Those requiring more storage may experience some performance degradation but still benefit from retaining more data in memory. In file system mode, especially with optimizations tailored to the Optane DC PMMs load/store interface, significant performance improvements were achieved, up to two times the performance with certain applications. Furthermore, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach, resulting in substantial time gains. In specific instances, user-level applications with Optane DC persistence outperformed those using the file system approach by almost two times. In situations where memory access patterns differ significantly from random, the Optane DC PMMs' bandwidth limitations are less of a concern, making them an effective persistence solution in those cases. Overall, our research confirms the value of Intel's Optane DC PMMs as a persistent memory technology, offering fast, byte-granular data access and reliable storage, particularly when used by user-level applications. In addition, our findings highlight the importance of optimizing software for the unique characteristics of Optane DC PMMs, especially its file system mode, to fully realize its potential. In addition, our research includes an open-source benchmark suite known as OptaneBench, which is available for download and can be used to evaluate the performance of various systems utilizing Optane DC PMMs. In the future, we anticipate a greater need for persistent memory technologies like the Optane DC PMMs, especially in applications with large datasets and intricate memory access patterns. Consequently, there will be a growing requirement for software optimization tailored to these types of applications, which is expected to significantly impact how computer systems utilizing persistent memory are designed and optimized. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, we suggest that this feature is an embryonic form of a more intricate phenomenon found in a related equation. The implications of this discovery are significant, as they suggest that even simple models based on autonomous agents exhibiting persistent behavior may give rise to high-dimensional turbulent patterns. In addition, we propose that the presence of these patterns could provide a explanatory framework for the emergence of high-dimensional turbulent patterns observed in other models. The design of the model and the analysis of the results are set within the broader context of understanding how persistent, cooperative behavior in complex systems could result from fundamental principles, and the need for further research in this area. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 alloys evaluated using the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg model and the Kubo linear response theory. GdSn3 and CmSn3 are found to display antiferromagnetic behavior, while GdxCm1-xSn3 exhibits a spin disorder that originates from competing exchange interactions. Our analysis shows that the spin disorder in GdxCm1-xSn3 can be adjusted through the concentration of Gd and Cm. Additionally, our results indicate that GdxCm1-xSn3 with x=0.5 possesses the highest magnetic ordering temperature. These findings can contribute to the design of magnetic GdxCm1-xSn3 alloys used in spin-valve type Heusler compounds.

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we discovered that high T center densities can be created without compromising spin properties, paving the way for the simultaneous achievement of high density T centers and narrow optical transitions necessary for efficient photon-spin interaction.
