A simplified computer model is used to investigate various global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere by simulating and experimenting with different rotation rates and temperature differences between the equator and the poles. To better understand these experiments, various factors are re-cast in dimensionless forms to define a parameter space in which circulation patterns are mapped and classified. Notable patterns and trends emerge when varying rotation rate, as well as the rate at which heat and motion are transferred and released in the atmosphere. Similar patterns in circulation are found to occur under both laboratory and atmospheric conditions, when the curvature of the planet is considered. Baroclinic waves that behave similarly to those observed on Mars appear under specific conditions of temperature differences and atmospheric stability. Extremely fast planetary rotation leads to the formation of multiple jet streams on the poles, similar to the multiple jet patterns observed in gas giant atmospheres, and results in varying distributions of heat in the atmosphere with different rotation speeds. Lastly, the implications of these findings are considered in relation to ongoing and future studies of global atmospheres.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In order to address the issue of class imbalance, we developed Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward yet scalable AL algorithm capable of selecting more evenly balanced data samples for annotation. Consequently, BASE outperforms random sampling consistently. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. 

In conclusion, our findings highlight considerable room for improvement in developing effective AL algorithms, especially on large-scale datasets. Moreover, the success of BASE, along with complementary studies, underscores the importance of considering data imbalance in the development of AL methods. The code for BASE is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/yousefyan/balanced-selection. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and the classical quantum Hall states in the bulk, resulting from the exceptional neutrality of the electron energy spectrum at the neutral point. Additionally, resistance versus magnetic field strength curves from both small and large-sized samples demonstrated neutral state-related resistance peaks at the neutral point, albeit with some differences. These findings shed new light on the neutral state's behavior in HgTe quantum wells.

Wireless communication systems can make significant contributions to preventing road accidents through alert message transmission, particularly in high-risk areas like road intersections. By comparing the ACN protocol to existing alternatives, we demonstrate that ACN yields a substantial improvement in outage probability at road intersections, particularly for higher data transfer rates. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations verify our theoretical findings. The ACN protocol's superiority can be achieved by adapting the ACN parameters to optimize performance or by incorporating additional technologies, such as orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM). The ACN protocol's robustness in real-world applications is also illustrated through simulations of varying traffic conditions and system configurations. The results indicate that the ACN protocol's outage probability is significantly lower than alternative methods and can support high-data transfers up to 8 Mbps at road intersections. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions.

Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors, particularly in their mixed-state Hall resistivity. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that vacancy activation energies are significantly lower than those of isolated vortex lines, offering a framework that could potentially inform and guide other research in this area. Moreover, this study provides quantitative evidence to establish the vacancy model as the theoretical framework that best explains the mechanisms underlying the Hall anomaly in type-II superconductors. This understanding of the vortex state, coupled with the knowledge of vacancy activation energies, could potentially be applied to other transport phenomena or those involving the interaction between vortex lines and other defects in superconducting materials. Researchers suggest employing high-order cumulants and factorial cumulants of conserved charges to investigate critical dynamics in heavy-ion collision experiments. A parametric representation of the 3D Ising model, which shares a universality class with Quantum Chromo-Dynamics, is used in this study to examine how the second to fourth-order cumulant values of the order parameter change with temperature, and regardless of an external magnetic field at the critical temperature, these normalized cumulant values are independent, resulting in a temperature fixed point. Furthermore, Monte Carlo simulations in finite systems confirm the existence of this fixed point at temperatures near the critical point. The fixed point is also found in normalized factorial cumulant behavior for at least fourth-order cumulants and is mapped into the QCD, resulting in a similar fixed point in energy dependence along different freeze-out curves in QCD. The shape of these curves resembles a finite system's magnetic susceptibility curve near its critical point, and both are independent of whether a system exhibits long-range order or not. Consequently, this fixed point may be considered a hallmark of critical dynamics in finite systems and could serve as a signature in experiments related to QCD. Additionally, this study implies that the ratio of fourth-order to second-order cumulant values will provide a robust indicator for identifying the critical point in experiments related to QCD. We extend a prior investigation by N. Sato, generalizing his findings to encompass the broader context of such squares. Additionally, we establish a characterization for such squares yielding a given type II_1 subfactor, and this analysis contributes to a broader understanding of 4-tensors related to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological systems. These charactersizations facilitate the identification of sufficient conditions for the existence of strictly block-scale invariant subfactors of type II_1, and we demonstrate the non-triviality of some of these conditions. We also establish a connection between strongly integrable boundary field theories and commutative squares of C*-algebras, reconstructing the quantum doubles of weakly integrable TTFs as strongly block-scale invariant, completely periodic subfactors. This process involves establishing the duality between strongly integrable boundary field theories and commutative squares of C*-algebras. We utilize this framework to construct new examples of strongly block-scale invariant subfactors of type II_1. We also establish the relationship between the strongly block-scale invariant subfactors and the strongly block-scale invariant boundary field theories, recovering the latter from the former through the fusion beacons. This process involves introducing the category of bulk observables associated with a given commutative square, and establishing the natural morphisms between them. We demonstrate that the hyperfinite subfactors obtained in this manner exhibit strong block-scale invariance, and can be viewed as the images of the chiral CFTs underlying the weakly integrable TTFs, whose quantum doubles are the strongly block-scale invariant subfactors of type II_1. We conclude by introducing the category of bulk observables associated with a given dual commutative square, and establishing the natural morphisms between them. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, results show that this approach surpasses traditional transfer learning in both aspects. Additionally, we analyzed the system's performance with different optimization methods and data augmentation techniques. We applied this method to an actual safety-critical dataset and observed significant improvements in both accuracy and reliability. Overall, our study demonstrates that this collaborative framework is an effective way to create more trustworthy machine learning models for critical situations. It not only increases both accuracy and reliability but does so with only a minor increase in training data, outperforming traditional transfer learning. Moreover, it has practical applications as evident from its positive results on the safety-critical dataset. This suggests that this approach has great potential for use in real-world scenarios. We also found that it can handle a wide range of errors, especially those caused by neural network errors, and easily scaled to various datasets with different characteristics. We have made the code and data associated with this study freely available for use by the research community. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. Furthermore, a practical demonstration is conducted on HiXray, where the model's sensitivity and specificity are evaluated under real-world inspection scenarios. The code and dataset will be made available to the community. Overall, our method offers a pioneering solution to prohibited item detection and can be applied to other difficult image classification tasks. 

Title: Prohibited Item Detection in X-ray Images with a Novel Lateral Inhibition Module

This paper introduces a novel approach called the Lateral Inhibition Module, which successfully tackles the challenging task of detecting prohibited items in X-ray images. The method incorporates a Lateral Inhibition Module that mimics the human ability to focus on distinguishing characteristics and disregard irrelevant information. This module includes bidirectional propagation and boundary activation modules, which emphasize identifiable features from multiple directions and minimize noise. Experimental results on the newly created HiXray dataset and OPIXray demonstrate that this method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection methods. Additionally, the code and dataset will be made available to the community. Moreover, the paper evaluates the model's sensitivity and specificity in a real-world inspection scenario. This approach offers a pioneering solution to prohibited item detection and can be applied to other difficult image classification tasks.

A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we establish the relationship between $J_n^T$, the colored Jones polynomial, and its counterpart in biperiodic links, and predict volume conjecture behavior for the latter hold true.

This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path. Further, the investigation is extended to the reciprocal gamma function's extension, leading to a novel representation of the Hankel transform of the second kind. Finally, the research is applied to derive a direct integral expression for the Coulomb scattering amplitude in center-of-mass coordinates. 

In Chapter II, a pure integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function is found in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. This representation is proven to be equivalent to the standard complex representation, followed by obtaining a modified complex representation after changing the Hankel contour to a standard one. The investigation is then extended to the reciprocal gamma function's extension, allowing for novel representation of the Hankel transform of the second kind. This new understanding is utilized to derive a direct integral expression for the Coulomb scattering amplitude in center-of-mass coordinates. 

It is notable that the reciprocal gamma function is typically represented through an intricate complex function in the mathematical community. A direct integral expression for it has not been obtained before. The reason for exploring the reciprocal gamma function is to obtain a closed expression for the Coulomb scattering amplitude in center-of-mass coordinates, which has been known only in the big-$b$ expansion until now. 

It is also worth mentioning that the Hankel transform of the second kind is an important operator in mathematical physics. It has been widely applied in partial wave calculations for Coulomb-scattered waves, Coulomb-exchanged kernels and Coulomb-field transformations. 

In addition, the study derives a closed expression for the Coulomb scattering amplitude in center-of-mass coordinates, providing a new perspective on this fundamental physics concept. The expression obtained exhibits a fascinating relationship with the Watson theorem. Moreover, due to its complex function nature, the reciprocal gamma function has numerous applications in various areas of mathematical physics and physics research. Therefore, it is hoped that the fundamental expressions derived in this study will be able to stimulate research in these areas. 

The study's novel integral expressions for the reciprocal gamma function and the Hankel transform of the second kind are its key achievements. The traditional complex representations for these functions are often obtained only after contour deformation in the complex plane. In contrast, the study has extracted a direct relationship between the two types of representation for the first time. It is anticipated that this new insight will lead to a fresh understanding of these fundamental concepts

The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, top quark single-production cross-section measurements were made in several ranges of kinematic conditions, with values ranging from 0.4 to 6.2 nanobarns, in line with theoretical predictions. These findings represent crucial milestones in the study of nucleon structure using top quarks at the LHC.

This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/zspsql. The study's data and results are shared online at https://yewang.me/zspsql/.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. Our music captioning framework combines a proposed audio feature extraction method using weighted spectral sub-band and a sequence-generation technique using a deep recurrent neural network. The audio feature extraction method significantly outperforms existing techniques to determine the most relevant acoustic features for music genre classification, as evaluated through the use of weighted spectral sub-band and a method assessing feature importance through pairwise interactions. The proposed music captioning framework shows promising results on the ML170 dataset, as demonstrated by metric computations for music captioning. Additionally, human assessment via crowd sourcing reveals that our approach yields descriptive captions considered clear and relevant by at least 80% of participants. The effectiveness of the proposed music captioning framework is further validated by comparative trials conducted on the Large Music Dataset, a significantly larger dataset. The code for the proposed music captioning framework is now available online via an open-source link provided.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. This new stochastic hydrodynamic framework provides a powerful tool for studying the intricate dynamics of interacting Bose gases.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. Visualize our method's performance on ActivityNet v1.3 at http://activity-net.com/challenges/2021/. Our method's performance on THUMOS-14 can be viewed at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN-Results.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in the JET tokamak's edge plasma remain somewhat enigmatic despite detailed documentation. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. Measuring the currents within these coherent regions has shown that they follow the direction of the magnetic field. Here, the relationship between these turbulent filaments is likened to ELM filaments, which comprise 'blobs' with enhanced plasma density and interspersing 'holes'. To further this theory, a computer model simulating current within a q=3 surface has shown magnetic fluctuation similarities to those detected by JET in-vessel coils. This implies that the manifestation of a PTM is closely linked to capturing 'holes' on such a surface post-ELM, producing corresponding signatures in magnetic field readings. Conversely, the detection of 'blobs' captured on a q=4 surface would produce the signature indicative of an outer mode, a variant of PTMs. This theory offers a unifying explanation for the distinct PTM modes seen before large ELMs and could provide a basis for predicting the outcomes of such events. Furthermore, it suggests that magnetic field fluctuations associated with PTMs can offer valuable insights into the behavior of ELMs. Lastly, this framework also suggests the existence of a previously unobserved 'inner mode' involving the capture of 'holes' on a q=2 surface. This could have far-reaching implications for our understanding of the interactions between plasma turbulence and the plasma boundary. In addition, this theory may also have a broader significance, addressing the long-standing question of how plasma turbulence maintains its persistent coherent structures across multiple scales. While this study has focused on the relationship between PTMs and ELMs, it is clear that a deeper exploration of this connection will also require a examination of the core plasma dynamics leading to ELM formation. Ultimately, this study hopes to have provided a foundation for a fresh perspective on the nature of PTMs, as well as a basis for a more comprehensive investigation into the underlying causes of ELM turbulence. This perspective has significant implications for a better comprehension of the complex plasma interactions at play in the edge region of the tokamak. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Modifying the variable repulsive force field to consider the velocity of nearby robots further enhances the vortex potential field method, and it's shown that this approach can be applied to a broader class of motion scenarios, including robots moving at different speeds in different directions. Moreover, it's argued that this method has benefits over other collision avoidance techniques, particularly in situations where robots have varying levels of autonomy, and it's also compatible with distributed implementation, but may suffer from slow response times in some cases. Lastly, it's suggested that further research is needed to tackle more complex collision avoidance scenarios, such as when robots are moving at different speeds in different directions, and to test the approach in real-world applications. The proposed method is evaluated on a mobile robot platform, and several modifications to the variable repulsive force field are presented, along with related discussions and future research directions. Given an independent and identically distributed sequence of letters broken down into words based on independent and identically distributed renewal times, an independent and identically distributed sequence of words is formed.  The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed.  The relationship between the two type of large deviation principles, where the quenched LDP corresponds to the large deviations for a Markov chain with a given initial distribution, is discussed, as does the extension of the identified laws to the laws of the stationary measures, which results in an interesting interaction between the two type of large deviation principles, especially when the underlying Markov chain is irreducible.  The technical requirements for the sequence of letters to satisfy the condition known as regular variation, which includes the case of power law tails, are analyzed, as well as how the defined laws are related to the Feller-Lyapunov type conditions, which provides the framework for the general discussion of the applied and theoretical issues involved. Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. To further validate our proposal, we conducted a systematic analysis of the NMC model's performance under various settings, including different benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, and base model alternatives. All code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/NMC baselines.

Approximately nine years ago, Azrieli and Shmaya introduced a category of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games where each player's payoff function is influenced by a $\lambda$-Lipschitz rate in response to other players' actions. Their work demonstrated that these types of games have the capacity for achieving $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$ settings. Despite their findings, they left unanswered the question regarding the complexity of obtaining such equilibrium points. Our work contributes a query-efficient conversion from broader classes of games to those defined as Lipschitz games, thereby allowing us to derive a lower-bound restriction for the efficiency of randomized algorithms in finding $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria in $n$-player games with binary actions and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties, with an exponential relationship between the complexity and the ratio of $\frac{n\lambda}{\epsilon}$. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of 'Multi-Lipschitz games' that incorporate distinct Lipschitz rates for each player, followed by a transformation from equilibrium-finding tasks within this broader class to similar tasks within the domain of $\lambda$-Lipschitz games, with implications on the sum of individual $\lambda$-Lipschitz parameters. Finally, we establish a lower-bound restriction indicating that deterministic algorithms experience an exponential increase in complexity in finding $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibria in $n$-player games with multiple action options and specific $\lambda$-Lipschitz properties for particularly restrictive $\epsilon$-value settings, thereby advocating the utilization of randomized algorithms in our previous analysis and further contributing to our methodological simplifications over prior work yielding comparable results. These contributions offer an exhaustive exploration of the complexity of finding approximate Nash equilibria within the specified game theoretic frameworks.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our study further offers concrete evidence supporting the j-k CV framework over traditional k-fold CV methods, as it enables greater stability in model performance and parameter selection, allowing for better generalization on unseen data. The experimental results show the variance component accounts for the majority of performance estimation's overall variability, as indicated by our proposed j-k CV framework. Moreover, we found employing j-k CV with J > 5 yields consistent and robust model performance, as evidenced by our experiments on the Wiki10-5000 dataset. In contrast, traditional k-fold CV methods proved unreliable and yielded model performance that was generalizable but often suboptimal. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives. It also offers industry practitioners and the academic community a comprehensive knowledge base that can inspire innovative research in this domain.

We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. We also established a crucial connection between our modifications to the optical Bloch equations and the properties of the atomic transition itself. Finally, we offered guidelines for adjusting experimental parameters to minimize the impact of photon recoil or take advantage of its effects, depending on the requirements of the investigation in question. Our findings are highly relevant to other ultracold species that exhibit similar atomic properties.

Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Additionally, this work has significant implications for understanding viscosity in the vicinity of shear jamming and may have a significant impact on research involving the mechanical properties of materials that exhibit shear thickening.

Our study shows that in a bilayer Heisenberg antiferromagnet, low-lying triplon
excitations may offer a suitable path to achieving magnetic analogs of twisted
superfluid and supersolid phases previously found in ultracold atomic condensates
trapped in optical lattices. Employing a cluster Gutzwiller mean-field theory,
we prove that Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions are responsible for stabilizing
these phases within a magnetic framework, whereas in ultracold atomic systems,
the required mechanism involves the pair hopping process. Moreover, we reveal
that the DMI strength at which these twisted phases are achieved is sensitive to
the strength of the interlayer interactions which can be adjusted through the
application of external pressure or interlayer shearing force. Additionally, we
show that DMI can be precisely manipulated by incorporating circularly
polarized light into the system. Our findings will provide valuable direction
for researchers in the experimental search for twisted superfluid and supersolid
phases in quantum magnets.

A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Additionally, motion compensation can be employed to enhance accuracy in estimation of organ deformation fields. 

This technique is open to enhancements, with potential for direct utilization in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI, also capable of mitigating limitations posed by respiratory motion.

This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex nonlinear control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of systems characterized by variable relative degrees. Finally, the paper showcases its efficacy through simulation examples in adaptive cruise control and spacecraft rendezvous. Moreover, it highlights the computational efficiency of ICCBFs compared to their HOCBF counterparts. Additionally, experimental validation of the adaptive cruise control feature is also presented. Furthermore, instructions on combining and verifying datasets are provided using the knowledge of shipping industry specialists and former top executives. A descriptive analysis of previously unstudied market phenomena known as the "container crisis" is conducted with this data. Structural changes in the data variables are then identified to demonstrate how the dissolution of shipping monopolies affected market behavior. A theoretical framework is then utilized to develop an econometric model, and the results of the model are used to investigate the market characteristics and structural changes further. Ultimately, an investigation of the profitability of shipping businesses is conducted with the data to gain insights into firm behavior and strategy within the industry. Lastly, implications of the research are discussed in the context of recent industry developments.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this safer estimator exhibits performance comparable to the classic estimator when dealing with diverse distributions, including normal and heavy-tailed distributions, across various dimensions and strengths. Notably, this improvement does not incur additional storage needs, nor does it alter the sketch size or any of its underlying components. As a result, this safety enhancement is seamless and universally applicable across all CountSketch-based algorithms. We also introduce a new sketching method inspired by the safety-enhanced estimator, which provides a simpler alternative to CountSketch, especially effective in scenarios with limited feedback, such as gradient descent in high-dimensional spaces. This new method demonstrates a safer estimator with linear query complexity, which further simplifies previous solutions by eliminating the need for intricate analysis of query distributions. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This estimation suggested that the anisotropy of the cylinder's drag experienced in granular materials could be predicted by taking into account the flow of sediment and the drag experienced by the cylinder in air. This prediction held true in beds with high friction but needed further confirmation in beds with low friction. The curvature of the cylinder had a significant impact on its drag experienced in air but little impact in granular materials. The drag experienced by a curved cylinder moving through a granular material was found to be similar to that experienced by a flat, long cylinder with a similar width and speed. This led us to suggest that the shape of a granular bed's intruder with a curvature greater than 0.5 could be considered flat over its entire width. The drag experienced by the flat parts of the cylinder was found to be a significant contributor to its overall drag, especially at low speeds, and was found to be influenced more by its depth than its speed. This led us to propose a new model that could be used to estimate the drag experienced by a long, flat solid moving through a granular material. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. As a result, BoAnon is an highly effective BO framework for auto-tuning computer systems. The methodology used by BoAnon is also applicable to other optimization domains with complex, structured parameters. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Yet, once accounting for kinematic dependencies, we found differential $v_3/p_T$ to be discrepant from $v_2/p_T$. These findings underscore the intricate relationships between initial geometry, flow phenomena, and intermediate interactions, which in turn influence the observed collective flow patterns. Lastly, we suggest that the distinct $v_3/p_T$ and $v_2/p_T$ profiles may indicate the existence of $p_\perp$-dependent fluctuations in longitudinal angle, albeit indirectly. Upcoming experiments such as the Large Hadron Collider's high-brightness beam delivery system, featuring precise pseudorapidity coverage, will provide valuable insights into initial conditions and the underlying mechanisms governing QCD, specifically through the anticipated detection of higher-order anisotropic flow in 5-10 GeV/h bins. This, in turn, will yield a more comprehensive understanding of heavy ion collisions. Nonetheless, our research already demonstrates the capability of the MPDT model to predict observable outcomes that align with data from the Large Ion Collider, including $v_2$ and $v_3$ in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Moreover, we have incorporated the proposed experiment's capabilities into the model development, allowing for precise predictions of a range of outcomes that will become available with upgraded experimental equipment. Specifically, we have incorporated precise pseudorapidity coverage, precise centrality control, and the capacity to distinguish flow in various pseudorapidity intervals. Furthermore, with future experiments likely to employ external particle probes, we have also incorporated support for charged hadron distributions across a range of pseudorapida values. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation. The paper also provides practical applications of the proposed method in conjunction with common models, such as autoregressive models, self-similar processes, and Mittag-Leffler processes, showcasing the method's effectiveness through simulations. Furthermore, the paper highlights the method's benefits in relation to real-world data, including income distributions and earthquake data. The associated computational costs are also examined to validate the method's practical applicability. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. The abundance of iron in the gas within one kiloparsec of these three galaxies is below typical values seen in Seyfert galaxies, with estimates at <0.26 solar units, which may indicate a low supply of iron due to gas flows within these specific galaxies. These iron abundance estimates also suggest a total iron mass of 0.3-1.3 molar units within one kiloparsec of Mrk 79 and a recombination timescale of a few tens to over a hundred years for iron in the gas within these galaxies. These outcomes support the concept that gas flows play a significant role in the ionization and temperature variations observed in close proximity to supermassive black holes. The large size and low temperature of the gas within one kiloparsec of these three galaxies also suggest that gas flows due to minor mergers could be responsible for powering jet engines in these galaxies through the providing of fuel to gas in close proximity to the supermassive black hole, which can then power jet flows that support the formation of dusty tori. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The framework's core features include a sophisticated logic-based testing language for safe and efficient experimentation, integrated tools for debugging and performance analysis, and a compact virtualization approach for reducing overhead during multi-platform testing. Frisbee has been successfully applied in the development and performance evaluation of an Energy-aware Stream Processing System, and its code is freely accessible on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. Further information can be found at https://frisbee-test.io/. Experimental evaluations conducted with real-world applications and published in our companion paper demonstrate Frisbee's performance advantages over existing testing solutions.

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. The code for this project has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yichunzheng/SceneGen. The accompanying paper can be found on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.02415. As a result, we are providing the code for the scene generator model used here, along with the sensor simulation pipeline, in the hope that it will be of value to other researchers working in this area. In addition, we are making available the simulation data created using SceneGen, along with the real data it was designed to mimic, in an effort to advance the development of more accurate simulation models. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures exhibit unique properties, such as bijective mappings and periodic behavior, leading to the derivation of new correlation inequalities. Additionally, we demonstrate the uniqueness of the free measure derived from the group representation, establishing a connection to a recent uniqueness result among integrable measures. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the representation of the Ising model and a certain stochastic process called the uniform random walk on the group, allowing us to conclude the uniqueness of the stationary measures for the Ising model and the uniform random walk on the group. Lastly, we discuss an intriguing open question related to the mixing time of the uniform random walk on the group.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by combining this new iterative method with an explicit Runge-Kutta scheme, the authors successfully preserve bounds, mean values and anti-diffusive properties in various numerical experiments. The proposed framework's efficiency is also confirmed by conducting computational cost comparisons with traditional approaches. We developed three-dimensional hydrodynamic models of superbubble formation to
study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star
clusters located within low-metallicity ($0.02Z_{\odot}$) molecular clouds.
Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles
to become irregularly shaped and driven mostly by expanding hot gas through low
density pathways. Our findings show that in large ($\sim 10^7M_{\odot}$) molecular
clouds hosting large ($\sim 5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot}$) superclusters, dust grain
growth contributes $4.8\times 10^{-5}M_{\odot}yr^{-1}$ to dust accumulation
over 2.5 million years. However, pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
increase dust supplies up to $\sim 1200M_{\odot} (M_{SC}/5.6\times 10^5M_{\odot})$, 
with $M_{SC}$ denoting the stellar mass of the supercluster. Consequently, dust
production by both grain growth and supernovae could lead to considerable dust
accumulation within low-metallicity molecular clouds, a process compatible with
galactic dust formation patterns during early cosmic reionization phases.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. For a static, spherically symmetric spacetime, research has focused on conformal matter collineations within the energy-momentum tensor. The overall structure of these collineations is determined under non-degenerate conditions, with fifteen distinct, independent forms found. However, when the energy-momentum tensor becomes degenerate, the associated conformal collineations exhibit infinite degrees of freedom. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. The code and benchmark data are publicly accessible on our project site.

This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we plan to enhance Timeloops by enabling it to handle system call learning for multiple services combined, often seen in real-world microservices architectures. The source code for this research is available under the Apache License 2.0 at our GitHub repository.

The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The model's performance is impressive, but it's crucial to acknowledge that soccer involves human elements that cannot be captured through data analytics alone. Still, our approach demonstrates the value of reinforcement learning in understanding the strategy aspects of soccer, and it paves the way for more comprehensive studies that incorporate additional aspects of the game. In particular, the model's state description can be adapted to explore other aspects of soccer, such as player positioning or team performance. Ultimately, our research offers a novel framework for analyzing the game and investigating fundamental questions about soccer strategy. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our study reveals that design optimizations 
can yield more optimal outcomes than those obtained through basic design 
considerations alone. Specifically, it was found that designing the phase plate 
with the electron beam's cross-section in mind yields better results than mimicking 
the geometry of the TEM's aperture. Additionally, our research demonstrates that 
complex designs lacking symmetry can offer comparable performance to simpler designs 
exhibiting rotational symmetry. The findings mentioned above are anticipated to 
significantly contribute to the enhancement of image quality in TEMs. Our study 
also includes explicit design recommendations for a TEM equipped with a 
programmable phase plate capable of attaining down to 1 Angstrom resolution. The 
associated software used in this research is also freely available online.  Our 
study ultimately offers over 100 design options for programmable phase plates, 
which can be downloaded from the Zenodo repository provided.  Our research is 
further supported by a data visualization featuring a series of probe size 
profiles corresponding to diverse design parameters.  Our study is conducive to

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This suggests that encoder representations hold a different character than traditional text generation quality metrics would suggest, highlighting the need for careful evaluation of models intended for interactive dialogue. As a byproduct of this research, a suite of evaluation tasks and benchmarks for encoder representations in dialogue models is introduced, available for further exploration and improvement by the community.
