Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To tackle this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections. The proposed network is tested and validated on the KITTI dataset, with experimental results showing its enhanced performance and loop-closure capabilities when incorporating attention layers. The study indicates that adding this attention mechanism yields more efficient loop closures and outperforms existing LiDAR-based place recognition approaches. Moreover, results suggest that encoder layers with middle depths exhibit the best mean performance and exhibit robustness to orientation variations, with code publicly available for review and replication. Nonetheless, pure attention-based models lack sufficient context and are not sufficiently reliable for autonomous applications requiring autonomous loop closures. To enhance autonomy in LiDAR-based place recognition, the study recommends the inclusion of sensory data from additional perception sensors, such as cameras, to complement LiDAR-derived context and enhance context awareness. Consequently, this research provides a foundation for further investigation into LiDAR-based place recognition and the exploration of multi-sensor systems in autonomous loop closures. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The presence of optical phonons breaks the linear dependence at higher temperatures, but even so, the thermal capacity remains quite large compared to other semiconductors, which we attribute to a strong interaction between the phonons and Dirac electrons. Phonon density-density correlations also reveal the presence of a thermal screening of the static compressibility at low temperatures, which, however, breaks down at higher temperatures due to the emergence of phonon effects. The calculated thermal capacity and compressibility are consistent with existing experimental data. Moreover, we offer a thermal screening hypothesis that could explain the disparate values of charge carrier velocity measured using thermal capacity and compressibility techniques. Our study provides a thorough theoretical basis for using doped graphene as a reference material for investigating room temperature phonon physics. It also offers a perspective on the field, anticipating breakthroughs when the rules of room temperature phonon physics are re-examined in the context of current theories of solid state materials. Lastly, our findings pave the way for further research on the interplay between phonons and Dirac electrons, which could lead to unique phonon-driven transport phenomena in graphene.

Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. Evaluations confirmed superior performance across multiple metrics. Notably, MaskedSpeech excelled in sentences with complex intonation patterns and 12-way emotion labels. Moreover, subjective assessments via user studies revealed increased user trust in the system. MaskedSpeech's code and data are openly available at https://github.com/academanyu/MaskedSpeech.

In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. 

In the realm of effective field theories, our findings reveal that the presence of multiple symmetries leads to the creation of an abundance of both standard and advanced Q-ball states, essentially independent of the underlying physics that drives the symmetry mechanisms. In contrast, the situation is markedly different in the case of first-order phase transitions, where the scenario is distinct and the standard and advanced Q-ball states share an identical field potential configuration.

The vast array of possible Q-ball states presents an intriguing challenge to our current computational capabilities, making it extremely difficult to carry out an exhaustive study across all possible Q-ball scenarios. Nonetheless, our exploration of the complex Q-ball field has the potential to unlock new perspectives in this field, while also highlighting the importance of understanding the underlying physics when interpreting the intricate Q-ball spectra.

Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Specifically, we establish the following results: (1) If the residual characteristic of Q is not 2 or 3 and there exists a real place in the Galois closure of K/Q, then the ring of integers in K is freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from G. (2) If the residual characteristic of Q is 2 and the associated 2-Aut group of the Galois closure of K/Q is isomorphic to A4 or S4, or if the residual characteristic of Q is 3 and the associated 3-Aut group of the Galois closure of K/Q is isomorphic to A5, then the ring of integers in K is freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from G. (3) Otherwise, the ring of integers in K is not freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from G, thereby extending a key result initially presented in the author's 2018 paper published in the Journal of Number Theory. The paper also provides a newly derived formula to calculate the rank of the additive Galois module associated with K/Q. The formula is based on a deeply analyzed examination of the Galois closure of K/Q, particularly concerning its 2-Aut and 3-Aut groups, along with a detailed examination of the architecture of the minimal field in K that is steamed and fully ramified over Q. The derived rank formula provides a novel approach to determine the Fanoian nature of K/Q, thereby establishing a previously unknown connection between the additive Galois module associated with K/Q and the 2-Aut and 3-Aut groups of the Galois closure of K/Q. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. We also introduce BART-based models that successfully handle
these difficult cases and expand the tested vocabulary to 300 words with
substantial semantic change. Ultimately, our results highlight the
limitations of contextualized methods in detecting diachronic semantic shift,
along with difficulties associated with static vs. contextual interpretations
of word meanings. We also examine challenges related to distinguishing between
synonym and polysemous words and address potential limitations of our approach
given the existing corpus data. We make available our dataset, models, and
code at https://github.com/awashiki/wwcc and await feedback to enhance the
challenge. The current version has been accepted to the 13th International
Conference on Computational Semantics (IWCS 2021).

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we establish upper limits on the decay constant of ultra-light pseudo-Goldstone bosons, setting constraints on their dark matter composition and influencing the predictability of their gravitational effects. This research provides a framework for a new sensitivity for future radio surveys, such as the Square Kilometre Array, by identifying suitable targets for redshift measurement based on their luminosity and considering potential biases due to selection effects. Ultimately, we evaluate the potential of detecting the scalar perturbation of the spacetime metric through gravitational waves, offering guidelines on suitable targets and alternative methods to enhance detectability. If future observations can verify the predicted relations between radio luminosity and black hole mass and spin, we propose that future radio surveys could accurately determine the mass and spin of individual AGNs. This would not only provide valuable cosmological information but also enable the study of the evolution of black hole growth and the behavior of their spin over billions of years. This research could also pave the way for a new sensitivity for future radio surveys and offer a framework for a novel approach to understanding the fundamental features of black holes, the ingredients of dark matter, and the behavior of gravitational waves. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, we propose that retinal IKNM could
serve as a crucial model for studying the interplay between spatial organization, movement, and cell fate choice in the
brain. By integrating our imaging data with computer simulations, we offer a possible explanation for the observed nucleus
distribution across the retina. Our model suggests that the unequal distribution of nuclei is caused by the random cell
fate choice of cells located at the upper surface, and that this equality is disrupted due to the tight packing of nuclei
at this surface. Additionally, our findings indicate that cell fate choice is influenced by the location of the dividing
cell within the vertical retinal column. If the cell splits at the upper surface, the two daughter nuclei will have an equal
chance of migrating to either layer, thus maintaining the uneven distribution. However, if the cell divides at the lower
surface, the two daughter nuclei will have an unequal chance of migrating to either layer, and this could contribute to
the eventual decrease in the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina. We propose that retinal IKNM could serve
as a valuable system for exploring the complex interplay between spatial organization, movement, and cell fate choice in
the brain. We believe that a deeper investigation of this system, aided by advanced imaging techniques and computer
simulations, may provide valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms governing the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. In turn, this greater understanding of retinal IKNM may offer a unique perspective on cell fate choice

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This problem is solved via an efficient convex optimization approach that leverages the Projection-Gradient algorithm, ensuring fast convergence, critically tailored to handle the specific structure and constraints of code patterns. This method not only provides a practical solution to the long-standing problem of code pattern design but also offers an innovative solution to the related problem of compressed sensing, enabling the precise reconstruction of compressed images with no information loss, as demonstrated by our results. This code pattern design approach opens up new avenues for the development of tailored reconstruction algorithms and could also contribute to a better comprehension of how the brain processes and encodes visual information, given its similarity to the brain's visual coding architecture. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Furthermore, our findings also indicate that polar active fluids can evade the detrimental effects of quenched disorders to move freely, contrary to the obstructions caused by polarizations of the particles that can be frozen in place. Additionally, our model predicts the existence of a frozen domain around each inclusion in the two-dimensional plane, and we calculated the exact dimensions of this frozen area as approximately $|\log \sigma|^2$, where $\sigma$ represents the size of the inclusion. We also derived the overall diffusion characteristics of an individual particle over time as being on the order of $|\log \sigma|^2$ in the two-dimensional space, and this result holds even when the inclusion is much larger than the hydrodynamic radius of the particle. We believe our hydrodynamic theory has significant implications for understanding the dynamics of the tail of the polar active fluid. We have also developed an alternative approach using the method of addition for our theory. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
Furthermore, we anticipate that this exceptional van Hove singularity 
will give rise to an emergent $z=3/2$ Fermi liquid behavior. 
We propose that strategic material design can both prevent this singularity 
from developing and restore the normal Fermi liquid state, exemplified by 
the substitution of barium for strontium in calcium strontium cobaltates. 
In addition, we predict that this singularity will recur across the phase 
diagram of these cuprate materials as the pressure is increased, 
eventually breaking down under high pressure. 
Our theory is supported by computational simulations. 
Our study indicates that even though the exceptional van Hove singularity 
is intimately connected with electron correlation, 
it can be understood and analyzed through the use of non-interacting Fermi surface models, 
thus offering a pathway to experimental discovery. 
In addition, we suggest that both theoretical and experimental investigation 
of this concept will provide additional insight into the physics of these cuprate materials. 
Our study is accompanied by computational simulations. 
Our study offers both the concept of the exceptional van Hove singularity 
and methods for both experimental and theoretical analysis of this concept.

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During testing, it revealed a significantly increased count rate of up to 150 kHz of neutron signals, which were induced by muon showers, in comparison to 0.3 kHz of direct neutron detection. Furthermore, we demonstrate the capability of this system to identify both the incoming direction and timing of individual neutron events with accuracy. This technology has the potential to contribute significantly to the understanding of neutron flux and spectrum in deep laboratories. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The algorithms used to rank the targets can be executed in a timely manner in relation to the duration of the telescope allocation, and are designed to accommodate changes to the target ranking based on real-time observations and data acquisition. The methods developed for the TKS can be applied to any survey that aims to investigate a large number of planets detected through transit photometry, and the associated data is publicly available at https://tdc.ipac.caltech.edu/TDC/Public/tdc_astro/. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Ultimately, a longer observation period is necessary to confirm the YORP acceleration in these asteroids due to the limited sample size, but the discovered YORP accelerations could provide valuable insights into the composition and thermal conditions of these asteroids. Additionally, the rotation rates of Toro and Geographos are no longer considered irregular, whereas the rotation period of 1992 SK remains uniquely high among near-Earth asteroids in the 1 km size class. As a result of these studies, more extensive observations of these asteroids are now warranted to detect further evidence of the YORP effect and possible connections to their formation and distribution within the solar system. The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Notably, we found no correlation between the time spent online and users' willingness to engage in political discussions. Our data suggests that social media can facilitate meaningful political engagement, with users willing to invest time in commenting on issues that matter to them. We further explored the idea that online political discussions can serve as indicators of offline voting patterns. Although our findings did not support this notion, we believe it is a topic worthy of further investigation in different contexts. Our study provides a foundation for examining online political discussions and votes in the context of multi-party systems, as well as in systems with dominant two-party politics. We also suggest incorporating the attention mechanisms from deep learning models into our proposed network architecture. By doing so, we may better capture temporary trends and focus on crucial issues. We are making our code and data available to facilitate advancements in this area. Through our study, we are also introducing a publicly accessible Instagram comment dataset, comprising 1 million comments related to politics, in an endeavor to stimulate further exploration into online political discourse. Ultimately, we are resolute in our conviction that social media can serve as a powerful means to engage citizens in meaningful political discussions, empowering them to make informed decisions in democratic elections. Consequently, we are committed to continuous monitoring of online discussions in relation to politics, as well as analyzing elections through the lens of social media, in an endeavor to contribute to the advancement of democratic societies. We are dedicated to yielding actionable insights to politicians and civic leaders, equipping them with the knowledge necessary to effectively utilize social media in democratic elections. Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine.

Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. A stabilizable boundary feedback controller is designed for the Navier-Stokes equations using a linear control scheme with an oblique boundary orientation. This control strategy is applied to the $n$th harmonic mode of a cavity with an oblique boundary on the $x$-component of the velocity field, resulting in the damping of the corresponding unstable oscillatory behavior. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. The proposed model offers a valuable tool for modeling strain-induced crystallization in polymers subject to mechanical and thermal changes. The model's capabilities in representing crystalline region formation, material degradation, and temperature change in cyclic loading tests demonstrate its effectiveness. The ability to predict material sample temperature and microstructure provides valuable insights for polymer material design and production process optimization. The proposed model can be an essential framework for modeling other materials with complex microstructures that undergo strain-induced transformations. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. All computational results were obtained using a tight-binding model and first principle calculations, with additional implications for the related materials Sb$_2$Te$_3$ and Bi$_2$Te$_3$ also considered. These findings are expected to provide valuable insights for the design and realization of the related phases of superconductivity in these materials.

One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Our findings show that our method can effectively utilize different types of noisy feedback that model real-world interactions. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Additionally, we establish that the introduction of suitable universality properties can guarantee the existence of model companions within specific classes of theories. Ultimately, our work demonstrates that the concept of model companions offers a meaningful framework for addressing fundamental questions in set theory.

This study establishes conditions and proof of existence for a modified Branson-Paneitz equation under Navier boundary conditions on a finite region of n-dimensional Euclidean space. Building on previous work of Raymond and Yang, we demonstrate that a weak solution can be found within the appropriate function space, enabled by the Sobolev inequality with Hardy term. Additionally, we investigate the compactness property of the associated operator and establish a regularity result for the solution by combining sub- and super-solution methods. These findings have implications for the convergence of a gradient flow under certain stability conditions. Notably, we prove that the associated operator is compact when $n \geq 5$, enabled by a novel application of Poincare's inequality with Hardy weight. Lastly, we explore an application related to an equation of Branson-Paneitz type.

We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback. This new knowledge source also offers opportunities for the development of more capable models of human language that can be evaluated through their ability to generate text that is consistent with the patterns and standards that are inherent to the language as observed in the data at hand. Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. We demonstrate how lattice simulations can determine the minimum virtuality for a photon needed for Bjorken scaling to apply to structure functions. Additionally, we explain the parton model representation of the structure functions within the Bjorken limit and assess its coherence. In line with typical DIS on protons, a kinematic parameter $x$ here directly represents the momentum carried by the partons, with its value spanning from zero to infinity. If the partons' momenta are parametrized as $x T u$, with $u$ being the four-velocity of the fluid and $T$ the temperature in its rest frame, the distribution of quarks within the non-interacting quark plasma follows $x \log(1+e^{-x/T})$. This expression embodies the interplay between thermal radiation and the discrete quark levels, exhibiting peaks at $x \approx \pm T$ and exhibiting opposing behaviors for $x$ greater or less than zero. The resulting quark contribution to the sum rules exhibits opposition in behaviors for moments with odd or even indices, with an indication that the influence of thermal radiation diminishes with rising moments. The simulations were carried out using 504 independent lattice configurations at a lattice spacing of 0.2 fm for both the temperature of 0.45 Tc and 0.45 Tc itself, with the outcomes being insensitive to the distinction. The outcomes for the sum rules are also compared with the (non-interacting) perturbative QCD results, and the duration for which the thermal radiation dominates the structure functions is estimated as approximately 5-10 times the temperature. The detailed study of the sum rules can provide valuable insights into the properties of the thermal medium, while also making it feasible to investigate the framework of the Mueller-Navelet dijet spectrum within the same context. While the output for the sum rules is insensitive to the dijet spectrum parameters, a minimum virtuality for photons can be determined, with it being set at approximately 0.45 GeV. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Additionally, our work showcases the importance of distinguishing local and global features in novel view video prediction. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zyyang920/novel-view-video-prediction. Our paper has been accepted into CVPR 2023.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In light of these findings, it is suggested that a reevaluation of air transmission risk models is necessary to ensure their accuracy in capturing the complexities of aerosol transport in confined spaces. In addition, the use of the 'well mixed' model is cautioned against, as it may overestimate exposure to airborne pathogens by as much as tenfold. In contrast, more sophisticated models that account for turbulent airflow and residual aerosol transport may provide a more realistic assessment of the risks associated with air transmission. As an example of this, in a hypothetical scenario where an infected individual on a bus breathes out virus particles at a rate of 20 liters per second, with a total output of 100 microliters containing 105 viral particles, it is estimated that, assuming no ventilation and no surface deposition, the number of viral particles reaching other passengers could potentially reach 42 in as little as 5 minutes, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of aerosol transmission in enclosed environments. The findings of our study are further illustrated by numerical solutions to a mathematical advection-diffusion model, as well as through computational simulations carried out with the help of the CFDFuelOpenFOLE CFD solver. In conclusion, the analysis of virus-laden aerosol transport in confined settings like buses has significant implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens in enclosed environments. In light of these complex dynamics, it is recommended that a one-size-fits-all approach to air transmission risk modeling be avoided, and instead, a more considered assessment of aerosol transport risks is undertaken, one that takes into account the unique factors influencing airflow and surface interactions in each specific environment. In addition, greater access to computational modeling tools and experimental studies of aerosol transport in confined settings is deemed necessary to further advance our understanding of this critical public health issue. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Moreover, we've introduced an novel concept of entanglement-based unclonable encryption, offering a fresh perspective on this topic. Our research presents several open questions and invites further exploration in this field. Our findings are substantial enough to warrant a revisit of copy-protection methods based on quantum cryptography. Our research consists of two parts, preceded by an overview of relevant background information, including a review of Broadbent and Lord's works, entanglement-based cryptography, and the concept of monogamy of entanglement. Further, we identify a critical value of the potential function, determining when it reaches a minimum or maximum. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We observed improved generalisation performance, specifically on datasets requiring significant shifts, such as the rotation of images. We demonstrated that using this approach prevents the formation of sharp minima in the loss function, which is responsible for improved generalisation. We also found that using larger models benefits from this approach more significantly. We offered an upper bound for the model's performance when using this approach and generalised it to the context of federal learning systems. We further showcased the approach's applicability to any type of neural network and highlighted its advantages of easily modifiable hyperparameters. We publicly released all code and data used in the experiments. 

Keywords: Neural Network Training, Lipschitz Continuity, Regularisation Methods, Generalisation Performance.

benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental measurements of the participants' interaction with the modified game revealed that our low-latency statistical model accurately identifies optimal parameter values that reproduce baseline gameplay under controlled conditions. This methodology holds potential for addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, particularly those involving conflicting requirements for physical involvement and subjectively enjoyable experiences. To facilitate replication and further exploration of this research, the associated data and methods have been made publicly available. Through this approach, we aim to contribute to ongoing discussions about the design of gamified systems and provide a framework that can be applied to other contexts involving the intersection of physical involvement and subjective experience. This framework is particularly relevant to the area of motor rehabilitation, but it may also be useful in addressing balance problems related to the design of gamified systems, especially in situations where the goals for physical involvement and subjective experience are in conflict. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be adapted to generate corrections for other processes involving vector leptoquarks. As a key aspect of this research, we provide a detailed explanation of the code's underlying physics and computational aspects. By utilizing this code, we can refine our understanding of the fundamental properties of vector leptoquarks and and clarify the possibilities for their detection at the LHC. As a key aspect of this research, we offer numerical predictions that can be referenced in the field. Specifically, we have determined the upper limits for the product of a cross-section and a branching fraction for the decay of a particular vector leptoquark, given its mass and coupling strength, based on the available LHC data. As an example, for a class of heavy particles with the name S4, we have found that, under certain conditions, their mass must be greater than 1.8 TeV (at a 95% level of confidence) in order to contradict the observed data. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Moreover, dose-escalation experiments demonstrated a notable capability of the uncertainty-aware framework to reduce radiation exposure while maintaining image quality. Overall, this new framework provides higher robustness when dealing with unfamiliar acquisitions and is highly conducive to adaptive dose optimization techniques. Consequently, it has the potential to reduce harmful radiation exposure during PET scans. A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The implications of these findings are considered in the context of the systems examined. The study's methods and metrics are also applicable to other advanced computer systems that analyze connections within the text. By providing a framework for comparing these systems, the study advances the debate over the role of CT in the analysis of coherence within the field of computational linguistics. This debate is further fueled by the public release of the data and methods employed in the study. This research is a preliminary step towards a theory that explains the coherence within the text, the connections within the text, the cognitive processes that underlie the systems that generate the text, and the interactions between these factors. By considering the questions of whether the system recognizes the connections within the text before the two statements are processed together, what factors influence the connections within the text, and how the systems' knowledge influences the coherence within the text, the study invites further research and discussion in the field. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Our new results are accompanied by a tighter bound showing that directed graphs can be converted into upward planar layouts in time O(n^2), where n represents the number of vertices. Additionally, we've established the NP-completeness of the upward planar layout problem for directed graphs with three or more sources. Our research provides the first known studies on the computational complexity and parameterized complexity of the upward planar layout problem. Our results feature comparisons with known lower bounds for specific graph classes. The development of parameterized algorithms enables the identification of specific directed graphs that can be represented in upward planar layouts, leading the way for further research on this topic. The techniques employed in this project have also demonstrated value in other graph layout problems. The issue of determining whether a directed graph can be displayed in an upward planar layout serves as a fundamental problem with significant implications for other problems, giving it considerable relevance in graph theory and related fields. The development of parameterized algorithms for this problem opens new avenues for understanding this problem and related graph layout issues. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The research discovered that the best model, composed of selected feature sets and evaluated on multiple datasets, yielded an average ranking loss of 11.69 and mean absolute error of 6.92 feet. To facilitate replication and advancement of this research, the data, algorithms, and model sources are available for public review and modification. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of more precise and adaptable indoor positioning systems by addressing the variation in signal intensity distance metrics. The diverse nature of these datasets also provides a valuable opportunity for replication, validation, and exploration of additional machine learning approaches. A study explores whether constructing such a structure around a black hole would be feasible and efficient in powering a civilization. Considering six potential energy sources, researchers found that an accretion disk, which can produce $10^{5}\,{\rm L_{\odot}}$ of energy, would be sufficient for an advanced civilization. Additionally, a Dyson Sphere could potentially collect energy from relativistic jets and increase its overall energy output fivefold. Calculations indicate that a Dyson Sphere constructed around a stellar-mass black hole in the Milky Way could be detectable with current telescopes using waste heat radiation in the ultraviolet to mid-infrared spectrum. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres. With many black hole candidates with suitable conditions waiting to be studied up close, over ten candidates for possible artificial structures are already waiting to be re-examined, including CYGNUS X-1, NGC 1068, and IC 43218. Further research is necessary to develop more sophisticated methods for distinguishing artificial structures from natural phenomena. Nevertheless, the possibility of discovering a Dyson Sphere, whether successful or failed, could significantly impact our understanding of the potential for life beyond Earth. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. In fact, with appropriately chosen filling patterns, beam breakup instability effects can be minimized to a level where threshold currents are only limited by other stability constraints. This, in turn, allows for greater flexibility in design choices, particularly when it comes to recovering energy from multiple beams. A proposed design, involving an energy recovery linac for proton synchrotrons, demonstrates the feasibility of this approach for feasible machine sizes. Finally, potential issues related to beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs remain open to further scientific investigation.

To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The intricacy of these models is significant, partly because existing detectors have been incapable of observing final state neutrons, which has led to significant systematic uncertainties. The implementation of 3D scintillator tracking technology in next-generation long-baseline neutrino experiments has improved detection capabilities by enabling event-by-event measurement of neutron kinetic energy resulting from neutrino interactions, thus providing valuable information for refining neutrino interaction models and reconstructing neutrino energies. Prototypes of these detectors have undergone neutron irradiation at the LANL beamline in both 2019 and 2020. The primary goal was to demonstrate the ability of neutron detection by comparing the total cross-sectional area of neutrons and scintillator interaction at 98-688 MeV, which was measured at 0.36±0.05 barn, in accordance with established external measurement standards. The breakthrough of directly observing neutrino-born gamma rays in 2020's prototype data experiments further confirms the capability of detecting low-energy neutrino events. The outcome of this research has validated the development of detailed models describing the interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei and has provided valuable information for recovering neutrino energies from detection data used in long-baseline neutrino oscillation experiments. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can learn from multiple demonstrations, adapt skills to various target points, avoid obstacles, and meet complex linear and nonlinear constraints. Our work also establishes connections to state-of-the-art motion planning methods, and we provide evaluations of our framework through joint trajectory planning for a 7-DoF robotic arm, demonstrating its effectiveness. Our study offers EKMP as a versatile skill learning framework that can serve as a foundation for future research in constrained imitation learning. The code for our project is available online at the address indicated.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. A novel class of superconductors featuring antisymmetric spin-orbit coupling and placed within a Zeeman magnetic field may be used to create fault-tolerant quantum computations via topologically non-Abelian states. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. The high singularity at the location of the doping concentration $x=p=0.17$ is supported by our observations of the increased magnitude of the peak in the density of states within the interlocked vortex lattice state compared to other doping concentrations close to $x=p=0.17$. The discovered transition and its underlying physics also provide a means by which to study the $d$-wave properties of superconductivity in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$.

The research detailed in this letter provides the scientific community with a comprehensive understanding of the interlocked vortex lattice state in the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$.

However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. Furthermore, this method allows for more realistic simulation of such sources and the study of their variability. Additionally, it may facilitate more effective observation planning by generating more accurate predictions of source variability based on their properties and then simulating the sources' behavior over different observation periods. While this proposal is an innovative way to enhance image quality and source detection, it also raises interesting questions about the relationship between machine learning models and their underlying data. In this case, the model's effectiveness is tied to its training set, which, to yield meaningful results, must include a diverse range of sources similar to those it is designed to detect. If not properly controlled, this can lead to biases in the model's predictions about source variability, which, based on a limited sample, may appear significant but are actually minimal. Despite this risk, this approach has great potential for machine learning to take full advantage of the vast quantities of data being generated by current and upcoming telescopes. If tailored to handle big data, this method could automatically identify sources and detect transient phenomena in real-time or provide realistic source simulations based on actual observations. If successful, this could significantly enhance our understanding of the sky and the sources within it. While there are many challenges to be addressed, this proposal marks an important first step in this novel pursuit.
