Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We provide concrete examples and empirical evidence of our proposed methods on graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, Boolean satisfiability, graph connectivity, and abductive reasoning. We observe that even though accuracy of approximation varies across different applications, the serial dictatorship mechanism remains a viable, generally acceptable solution for addressing combinatorial optimization challenges in complex multi-agent systems. We also introduce a new concept, namely cooperative combinatorial auction design, based on novel game-theoretic considerations. We model and solve specific instances of these new challenges, delivering effective solutions in accordance with predetermined combinatorial optimization goals. We also examine various fairness conditions and discuss possible ways to achieve them with relevant incentive mechanisms. We offer concrete examples and empirically verify our proposed solutions on specific applications, guaranteeing acceptable social welfare in various combinatorial optimization domains, ultimately validating the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions derived from action sequences. We also introduce a novel metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences, and provide concrete evidence of our proposed methods on graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, Boolean satisfiability, graph connectivity, and abductive reasoning. We conclude that the serial dictatorship mechanism remains a viable, generally acceptable solution for addressing combinatorial optimization challenges in complex multi-agent systems

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. From a dataset of 4599 selected asteroids across 4342 images, our 
methods identified 19 potential wide binary prospects, including one identified 
asteroid with an estimated diameter of 13 kilometers. One such identified 
binary, specifically 2019 AC5, was confirmed via ARISS at the Mauna Kea 
Observatory. By reconstructing the asteroid's trajectory and examining its 
components' ratios, we were able to determine the orientation of its spin 
axis.Orbital analysis of the discovered binaries revealed that most of these 
wide binary asteroids occupy unstable orbits, whereas their smaller diameter 
counterparts more frequently reside in stable orbits. Moreover, we derived 
masses for four binary asteroids, and the resulting distribution of asteroid 
masses aligns with that predicted by the current gravitational scattering model. 
In conclusion, our study highlights the capability of conducting PSF 
analysis across wide field surveys, allowing the discovery of additional 
wide binary asteroids that can clarify binary stability constraints and 
enhance asteroid mass comprehension. As such, we encourage the review of 
existing wide field survey data using the described analysis techniques. 
Furthermore, we propose the adoption of specific targeted observations to 
uncover more wide binary asteroids, specifically focusing on previously 
identified prospects. As the number of confirmed wide binary asteroids

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  It led to unusual patterns observed in seismic data, and helped predict exploration findings in the S~ao Paulo Basin.  Those predictions include discovering hydrocarbon reservoir rocks in the S~ao Paulo High, and finding salt basins with thick salt deposits in areas with high strains and low velocities.  Additionally, predictions include finding sedimentary rocks in the Western S~ao Paulo Basin and along the S~ao Francisco Craton's conjugate boundary, as well as predicting areas with thin salt or no salt at all in the NE S~ao Paulo Basin.  These predictions have already been confirmed by actual findings.  They have discovered significant oil reserves in the S~ao Paulo High, specifically in the Alto Cabral, Caravelas, and Marlim fields.  Furthermore, they have discovered layers of sedimentary rocks, including sandstone and limestone, in the Western S~ao Paulo Basin and along the S~ao Francisco Craton's conjugate boundary.  Additionally, they have discovered thick salt deposits in high strain areas, such as in the Central S~ao Paulo Basin.  These discoveries support the model of conjugate boundary development presented in this study.  It highlights the significance of analyzing the history of extension and conjugation

A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images. 
Notably, our method achieves a notable improvement of 4.9% in the average
Dice score on the MindScope dataset and 13.8% on the Liver-11k dataset,
both with only 1% annotated data used.  Moreover, our approach exhibits a
notable advantage in robustness against different initialization methods,
confirming the inherent capability to learn meaningful unsupervised segmentations.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Additionally, we uncover that incorporating a Dopamine-like reinforcement learning mechanism enhances the DMD's overall performance. The successful implementation of a Dungeon Master informed by a theory-of-mind for the players paves the way for further exploration into how natural language understanding can be shaped by explicit objectives and the development of more sophisticated Dialog Management Systems that capture the intricacies of human social interactions. The code and data used in this project are now available at https://github.com/hahnfrid/dnd-socials. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through both rigorous model tuning and official evaluation on the SemChange dataset, yielding exceptional results when compared to established baselines. Furthermore, our approach has been made publicly accessible on our GitHub repository. Alongside, we introduce the LExiC repository, featuring comprehensive tools and code for both change detection and discovery, along with newly developed datasets and models. The republic also includes previously unexpected findings on German lexical semantic change. Unlike previous studies which primarily focused on type-based analysis, our work showcases the prevalence of token-based change and highlights the critical role deriving strategies for both change detection and discovery have in producing reliable results. Moreover, our study provides initial insights into the categorization of newly identified words with changing meanings. We discuss their physical significance and explain how they can be extracted from measurable DHFFs. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between these functions and the Boer-Mulders function, clarifying their distinct roles within the spin structure of the nucleon. The Boer-Mulders function is associated with the correlation between the movement of a nucleon and the spin of a quark within a nucleon, whereas the proposed functions are connected to the correlation between the movement of a quark and the spin of another quark within a nucleon. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This study demonstrates that the folding of knotted proteins can be understood at a native state level through intrinsic topological analysis. Moreover, it highlights the value of using knotoids, a more comprehensive framework that encompasses both intrinsic and extrinsic properties of knotted objects, in gaining insights into the complex folding processes of proteins. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a deeper investigation of folding pathways of proteins with trefoil knots by advanced simulation techniques. The methodology presented here can also be applied across various knotted proteins and potentially other macromolecules. The data and findings reported in this study are a crucial step in the ongoing quest to comprehend the intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes. The statistical analysis and simulation results reported in this study are made publicly available through interactive visualizations hosted on the NGL viewer platform. The source code for the visualizations and the underlying data are freely accessible on GitHub. The research presented here is further accompanied by a comprehensive review of the fundamental principles of protein knotology. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Additionally, we investigated the stress of existing structure on the EDE density, and found that it has a modest impact, with a density ratio of $f_\mathrm{EDE}(z=0.4)/f_\mathrm{EDE}(z=0.4)$ ranging from $0.9$ to $1.1$. As a result, EDE profile likelihood and density distributions agree with earlier findings, yet the methodology used here yields a more precise parameter estimate and reveals subtle EDE density variations across redshift. Consequently, models with $f_\mathrm{EDE}<0.1$ are now viable to resolve the Hubble tension, and could be confirmed or rejected with upcoming structure and cosmic microwave background experiments. Lastly, we highlight the importance of accounting for volume effects in EDE parameter choices, and stress the necessity of unbiased statistical analysis in such research.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. Although the hypothesis remains an open question within number theory, it has been shown that the anomalous NG theorem exhibits a phenomenon akin to random matrix theory's spectral symmetry. The implications of this finding are significant, as they suggest that the anomalous NG theorem could provide a bridge linking quantum field theory to number theory. The proposed framework for understanding the anomalous NG theorem has been set within the context of an invited talk presented at the 10th Aix-Marseille School of Mathematical Physics, where the relationship between quantum field theory and mathematical physics was explored. The associated proceedings have been published in the form of Lecture Notes in Physics volumes 883 and 884. The anomalous NG theorem has since been the subject of several papers that have further elaborated its fundamental principles and provided additional examples from a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios. The initial investigation presented here remains a foundation for these subsequent studies.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. The code and data produced by the DISCO framework are now available at https://github.com/mccarthy59/disco.

obtained results for the equality case of total, equitable, and neighborhood sum distinguishing
coloring when considering the degree sequence of these circulant graphs. We then compared
our findings with existing total, equitable, and neighborhood sum distinguishing coloring theorems.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy. Lastly, this study demonstrated that some Heusler compounds possess a strong tendency to rotate their lattice to match that of graphene, rather than adopting the epitaxial relationships found with bulk substrates. The ultimate outcome of this research is the successful fabrication of a spin-valvet switch using the epitaxially grown GdPtSb on LaAlO$_3$ substrate, remotely deposited on graphene. This device exhibits the desired spin-valvet behavior. The combination of a deep valley and a large spin-orbit coupling in this material are proposed as potential reasons for the observed spin-valvet phenomenon. The research further suggests that remote epitaxy offers a novel pathway to compound semiconductors with unique properties, offering hope for the development of functional devices such as spin-valvet switches and valley-specific photodetectors. Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The associated code is freely available at https://github.com/ashfaj/ cardiac_auscultation.  The project, which includes the dataset, can be accessed via https://github.com/ashfaj/cardiac_auscultation_data. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
This research also involves an informal discussion about the sequence reconstruction
problem's relationship to the copy problem, as well as a proposal for using graph theory
to tackle the sequence reconstruction problem in a more general sense. 
Additionally, we contribute an open-source programming tool designed to compute the
maximum possible overlap between two spheres in any given metric. 
This computation tool allows us to derive an exact value of the minimum number of channels
required to recover a transmitted sequence, which is 5. 
This result, in turn, enables us to devise an efficient protocol using 5 transmission channels. 
This protocol has the added benefit of ensuring exact replica transmission with at most 2 error types and a total error rate of 4.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This is evident from the results on the new dataset of audio excerpts representing 24 types of instruments, with only one-fourth of the classes being used for fine-tuning in a few-shot learning setup. Moreover, our proposed method proves more effective than a competing hierarchical approach that employs a multi-task design. We also investigate various strategies for selecting prototypes at each level of abstraction and present an approach that, through backpropagation, allows for the automatic adjustment of weights assigned to the hierarchical loss function. This project is backed by experimental data, showcasing how the introduction of new classes with a hierarchical structure aids the network in a few-shot learning setting. We've developed a dataset that can support the evaluation of future research on this topic and have made all code and data publicly accessible. The results we've achieved, coupled with the benefits of model interpretability that come with hierarchical organization, provide a strong foundation for using deep learning in additional applications involving the classification of musical instruments. This includes identifying instruments within audio tracks across different genres, such as jazz, classical, and folk, as well as identifying instruments within video game audio across various games. This research has the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of the sounds produced by different instruments and could ultimately aid developers in creating more realistic audio in video games. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code, data, and experiments are available at https://github/qasper.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, researchers, policymakers, and analysts must collaborate closely to tackle this global public health crisis effectively.

We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. This study thus provides an initial glimpse into the thermodynamics of Majorana fermions. This work is an extension to similar studies conducted with other types of fermions. The inherent self-entanglement of Majorana fermions results in distinct thermodynamic effects that differ from those of other fermions. This difference ultimately arises from the self-entanglement, which in turn allows for the flow of entropy despite the absence of particle conservation. This phenomenon produces unusual thermal equilibrium where both particle and antiparticle states coexist. This unique state is further modulated by the external linear potential through a change in entropy's distribution. This potential also modifies the thermodynamic properties by introducing a potential difference between particle and antiparticle states that can be detected at thermal equilibrium. This effect highlights the importance of considering the interconnection between particle and antiparticle states when analyzing the thermodynamics of Majorana fermions. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. This project's code contributes a key aspect to the community's efforts to advance the evaluation of abbreviations, as demonstrated in the recently proposed BACon evaluation criteria. Ultimately, we hope this system will facilitate collaborative research aimed at resolving the acronym identification and disambiguation challenge. This project has been developed using Python 3.7, Flask, Flask-Limiter, SpaCy, and Senna, and is compatible with the Ubuntu 18.04 operating system. The project has been supported by the University of Oregon's Shared Research Resources (ERRC) and the funding from University of Oregon's Inclusive Research Grant. In addition, we would like to extend our appreciation to the researchers selflessly contributing their data and expertise to this project. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. In the non-adabatic case, we derived a complex kick-driven pendulum model. Both models provide valuable new insights into the dynamics of atom-molecule systems. In the absence of collisional spin exchange, we were able to offer a simplified explanation for kick-driven oscillations. In the absolute zero temperature case, we found that type I superfluidity in molecule condensates cannot occur; however, we proposed a general framework for evaluating the excitation of molecule condensates through this conversion process. Finally, we explored the applicability of these theories to actual experiments. In the case of the MIT group led by Steven Chu, we found that a type I superfluidity phenomenon might be observable in a future experiment involving a spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes the need for more precise modeling of artificial materials and more robust methods for analyzing their momentum space properties. This review also highlights promising avenues for further research in this field. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Experimental results show MAG-Net's high accuracy across tumor types and views, demonstrating its potential as a reliable, real-world brain tumor diagnosis system.  With further testing and validation, the model could provide radiologists with valuable insights and enhance tumor detection in clinical settings.  Code availability: https://github.com/ashishghosh2/MAG-Net; Data availability: https://figshare.com/projects/Brain_Tumor_dataset/19960. The data used in the study is a non-annotated dataset, thereby radiologists' interpretation cannot be compared; instead, the model's performance is evaluated using metrics such as accuracy, loss, F1-score, and Dice coefficient. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this system permits us to learn a starting point for these variables from synthetic data, leveraging both ground truth annotations and the shadow visibility model. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach by recovering multiple scene properties from a single image containing a rigid object and a deformable character model, and also showcase the limitations of this system when dealing with multiple light sources and occluding objects. Our project page is available at https://virtualrac.net/projects/sphrender/.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. The proposed system's code is openly available online. This research provides a single-GPU-based solution for automatically restoring interlaced footage to progressive format at high quality, capable of processing videos with up to 1,920 x 1,080 resolution in real-time.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. Notably, our study employs a novel economic evaluation metric that balances precision with computational expense. The proposed probabilistic framework further enables the generation of uncertain flow velocity predictions, which is illustrated through an example of a flooding risk assessment. Overall, this research offers an innovative solution for high-performance river flow velocity prediction, addressing both the efficiency and accuracy shortcomings of traditional numerical methods. The associated code is publicly accessible on GitHub under the license CC-BY 4.0. The data is available on the U.S. Geological Survey’s (USGS) website. Future work will focus on enhancing the solver and applying this framework to additional water dynamics equations. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future. This approach also offers a potential solution to the challenge of scaling up catalytic reactor design. This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work. It also establishes that the stable map functions from a surface of genus greater than zero to the base of a fibered surface of genus one are categorized by the set of colored subgroups of the surface modulation group, which has previously been predicted by Benson Farb. It further explores the implication of this classification on the conjecture of Thurston regarding the classification of surface homeomorphisms that have a particular property. It shows that if a surface homeomorphism has a specific action on the colored subgroups of the surface modulation group, it is topologically equivalent to a homeomorphism on a surface with a cut, provided that the homeomorphism is not hyperbolic, and has a specific rate of divergence or contraction. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. Findings demonstrate that both BDDC and AMG can effectively solve complex cardiac mechanics problems, although AMG is found to be slightly more efficient for this application. Additionally, the research highlights the importance of thoroughly evaluating the performance of iterative solvers for complex problems, and suggests that BDDC may offer a more versatile solution for solving these types of equations on a variety of grid sizes. The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Moreover, our findings facilitate Conjecture 1.18 from the 2015 Combinatorial Challenges book edited by Jiri Havlicek. To establish the required spectral flipover property, novel techniques have to be developed, involving a recursive description of partition dynamics that guarantees convergence. This approach ensures that the spectral distribution has a robust limit, thereby enabling applications to random matrix ensembles with independent entries that are not necessarily uniformly subgaussian. The established limits also give rise to several new results, including the convergence of improved empirical eigenvalue distributions with various weights. Additionally, this convergence implies the almost sure convergence of the largest eigenvalue and corresponding empirical eigenvalue distribution in the large $n$ limit. Furthermore, the results can be extended to matrices with complex entries and with a focus on the counting problem of distinct empirical eigenvalues. The theoretical findings are further illustrated through numerical examples and simulations. The developed techniques have a broader impact, enabling numerous applications and result extensions. The full proof is provided in the companion paper by the same authors. The work is also relevant to recent advances in random matrix theory. The authors are grateful to N. Shiyu for the simulation codes and N. Shiyu, X. Sun, and J. Huang for the counting problem discussions. X. Sun and J. Huang also contributed to the combinatorial problems and the development of the recursive description. Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Given the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of producing such high-quality videos by professional teams, the field of AI-powered video creation has gained momentum. This field is unique due to its interdisciplinary nature, which presents a significant hurdle for researchers who are new to the subject. A current void exists in comprehensive surveys on AI-powered video creation, which is an area we aim to address through a thorough review of applicable AI techniques and the development of a taxonomy that breaks down the process into three distinct phases. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and extent of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. This, in turn, has significant implications for adversarial defense systems, given the critical role that gradient masking plays in existing scenarios. As such, there is a pressing need for alternative strategies that can provide robust protections against sophisticated adversarial attacks. This research includes both theoretical and practical components, with results validated through comprehensive experiments involving a range of neural network architectures. The associated code is freely available for download at https://github.com/hubwong/quantifying-gradient-masking. This study offers critical insights into the nature of gradient masking and lays the groundwork for a critical reevaluation of adversarial defense systems in machine learning. Recently, proposed bianisotropic acoustic metagratings offer promising possibilities for passive acoustic wave manipulation, notably in flat acoustic lenses and ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Advances in two-photon polymerization now enable precise manufacture of sub-wavelength structures in this range. However, shrinking structures in size introduces another challenge, where increased thermoviscous effects lead to considerable energy losses, which need to be factored into the design. This work introduces three novel microacoustic metagrating designs capable of refracting normally incident waves by approximately 35 degrees at 2 MHz, utilizing shape optimization techniques and the linearized Navier-Stokes equations. Using two-photon polymerization, we fabricated and experimentally validated microscopic acoustic metamaterials, successfully redirecting incident waves and verifying that a 0.29 wavelength-thick microacoustic metagrating can efficiently allocate 90% of transmitted energy into the -1st diffraction order. This breakthrough paves the way for optimizing microacoustic structures for specific applications and frequencies, enabling innovative acoustic wave manipulation in the MHz range. This, in turn, may lead to groundbreaking advancements in ultra-high frequency ultrasound imaging and other acoustic technology applications. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Through analytic and numeric methods, we demonstrate that the diversity of diffusion behaviors gives rise to distinct diffusion states that can be categorized into three primary groups based on the rate of mean squared displacements growth: sub-diffusive, linear, and super-diffusive. The time-dependent mean squared displacements can be predicted by a universal function of a dimensionless variable that combines the effects of correlations, variations, and time, enabling the classification of any self-similar diffusion process into one of these three categories. Furthermore, we introduce a new metric that distinguishes between stationary and non-stationary diffusion processes. The validity of our approach is verified through simulations of a two-dimensional fractional Brownian motion with a non-stationary Hurst exponent, where the population's spatial distribution reflects the influence of correlations and variations on a timescale defined by the exponent. The approach provides a robust framework for classifying a broad range of self-similar diffusion processes into sub-diffusive, linear, or super-diffusive states based on the rate of mean squared displacements growth. The methodology also offers a time-dependent prediction for the mean squared displacements and introduces a new metric that distinguishes between stationary and non-stationary diffusion processes. The validity of these predictions is demonstrated through simulations of a two-dimensional fractional Brownian motion with a non-stationary Hurst exponent. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. The complementary results show an intriguing correlation between improved calibration and uncertainty reduction in the extra dimension. Additionally, source code for this work is openly available.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The source code for this experiment management system, including the L2Explorer environment, is now available under an MIT license. To further contribute to the field, we're inviting researchers to join us in exploring L2Explorer, and we look forward to collaborating on this initiative. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Despite the potential for processes to include loops and deadends, our algorithm simplifies process reformation by focusing on natural decision points, making it suitable for various business applications. Moreover, it facilitates processes to be executed in real-time from data trails, offering an event-driven approach that improves process flexibility and scalability. This method is particularly useful when data trails are incomplete, as it can partially capture processes and later complete the data. This represents an important advancement in flexible process discovery, addressing prominent challenges in the field.

In one-dimensional quasiperiodic structures, certain types of wave propagation exhibit a sudden shift from localization to non-localization. Our theory and experimental results indicate that in one-dimensional photonic quasicrystals, light localization can transition back to non-localization at higher quasiperiodic modulation strengths for some states, representing an unusual phenomenon. Additionally, this occurrence can be understood through a mathematical model that represents dimerized interactions over extended distances. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that higher energy states display more precise dimerization and are less affected by a transition, whereas lower energy states react more strongly. This state-dependent dimerization and its consequences could provide valuable opportunities for manipulating light within these structures. Furthermore, our study identifies that dimerized states are more robust against perturbations, such as defects, which could enable more reliable transmission in these systems. Our results consist of analytical modeling and experimental data from optical waveguides consisting of a two-dimensional silicon membrane with etched Airbridge structures, offering a potential for scalable production. Optical systems that measure intensity in the far field are constrained by the Rayleigh criterion, a resolution limitation imposed by the system's aperture. Research has shown that using spatial mode demultiplexing (SPADE) allows for maximum collection of field information, thereby surpassing the Rayleigh criterion in certain cases. While previous SPADE approaches have relied on resolving the lateral splitting of a Gaussian wavefunction, our work investigates a novel scenario in which one of two photons from a bi-photon source, generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, undergoes a horizontal separation. Through coincidence measurements following the projection of both photons onto Hermite-Gauss modes, we demonstrate the ability to super-resolve this separation, a capability not attainable via standard SPADE techniques. Furthermore, our approach enhances the associated Fisher information by a factor of $\sqrt{K}$, where $K$ represents the Schmidt number that quantifies the entanglement between the two photons. Our findings indicate that SPADE of this type can provide a more efficient means of achieving the Heisenberg limit in interferometry experiments sensitive to phase shifts, particularly when a strong source-field correlation exists. In addition, our study reveals that SPADE of this type can offer a greater than $10^{10}$-fold improvement in the Heisenberg limit in experiments utilizing SPADE alone, a level that could significantly impact the realization of the Heisenberg limit in experiments with strong source-field correlations. Lastly, our work proposes and analytically models a novel SPADE scheme based on the projection of bi-photon states onto topological modes, which could enable the development of topological quantum information processing systems utilizing spontaneous parametric down-conversion. Ultimately, our research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to any SPADE system utilizing correlated photon sources, and highlights the unique capabilities and limitations of such systems. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Additionally, an analysis of the underlying dynamics in the vicinity of the singular Hopf point allows for the interpretation of the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the context of the full model. Finally, this research demonstrates that, in a system experiencing a singular Hopf bifurcation, the mechanism underlying mixed-mode oscillations can result from the interaction between the singular point and the surrounding invariant circle. This allows for the reduction of the model to a suitable normal form, located at the singular point, and facilitates an in-depth analysis of the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the context of the full model. This knowledge may be applied to systems experiencing other types of singular bifurcations, such as a singular torsade bifurcation, as demonstrated in the presented ecosystem model. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is demonstrated by bulge construction, combined with massive quiescent, lopsided galaxies in the current stage, until they collide with a major merger galaxy. Our research offers a novel perspective on galaxy evolution through accretion, and the complex interplay between core and disk systems. It also highlights the significance of optical classification, together with a study of the physical properties of optical counterparts, to better comprehend the evolution of galaxies through various processes such as star-formation, quenching, merger, and interaction. This has far-reaching implications for the construction of the next generation of submillimeter and far-infrared telescopes. This research is part of the ALMA-GO program ALMA-20120701-D (PI: C. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and can be classified in a specific way when these conditions are met, resulting in some of these solutions maintaining the same symmetry as Q(y). Additionally, we find that "bubbling solutions" will not exist under alternative circumstances when Q(y)'s local minimum is zero, specifically in instances when it does not equal zero. These findings are achieved through the application of minimization techniques, the definition of an appropriate functional, and the development of an associated Reedy stratification. We also derive an important estimate on the number of its "bubbling solutions" for this equation by establishing a connection to the number of local minima in Q(y). We end by discussing the case when Q(y)'s local minimum is not zero, giving a more precise analysis of its "bubbling solutions" when it is sufficiently small near zero. All "bubbling solutions" can be characterized as time-periodic solutions to the corresponding Navier-Stokes equation when Q(y) is not identically zero, and their sizes are determined by the values of the singular weights, W_\lambda. This research was inspired by the work of Shatah and Struwe, which investigated corresponding situations for the Navier-Stokes equation. Additionally, our approach allows us to establish the symmetry of these "bubbling solutions" directly, not relying on an inductive argument. We also explore "bubbling solutions" for a related equation that includes the square of the unknown function, which is not considered in the work of Shatah and Struwe. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with complex tasks, like entire function code production. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static code analysis for weak supervision. Our neuro-symbolic method allows a deep generative model to leverage a static-analysis tool to identify code connections generated, and trains on this data to generate code based on this analysis during training. When tested on the task of creating full Java functions within existing classes, our results reveal our approach outperforms state-of-the-art transformer models and a method that tries to learn program meanings, exceling at error-free code production and matching actual code structure. Furthermore, we found our approach to be highly versatile, supporting the development of new Java features and even enabling a deep generative model to assist with code debugging. The underlying technique we've introduced also provides a potential framework for other code generation tasks. The code and findings have been openly shared and can be found at https://github.com/ghori123/CodeGenerationWithStaticAnalysis.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Studies of November 7th, 2004 events offer insight into the complex nature of solar physics and the rare occurrences of solid evidence for solar neutron decay, a phenomenon that can only be observed at high altitudes with suitable detection systems. Moreover, it is implied that recovery of data from modern spacecraft during significant solar events may be crucial in understanding the underlying processes of these events. Additionally, it is suggested that re-examination of data from past solar flare experiments, along with newly discovered evidence, may provide a window into the fundamental nature of matter and the operating characteristics of particle physics at the extreme conditions found in solar plasmas. Finally, it is proposed that a dedicated satellite, centered around detection of solar neutron decay, could serve as a key component for understanding the most profound mysteries of the universe, specifically those related to solar physics, astronomy and fundamental particle physics. The construction of such a satellite is seen as a feasible goal that could be achieved through the collaboration of space agencies and particle physics institutions. The November 7th, 2004 events offer a perfect opportunity to initiate this initiative and provide a comprehensive report on the discovery and related discussions.
