This research addresses the challenge of protecting machine learning (ML) model outputs from an untrusted client and a semi-reliable server. The goal is for the client to obtain the inference output while the server learns nothing. Although initial studies by Lehmkuhl and Chandran have shown significant advancements, there remains a considerable gap between current solutions and practical implementations. To address this issue, our proposal SIMC 2.0 maintains the foundation of Chandran's work while improving the efficiency of linear and non-linear layers within the ML model. Key innovations include a customized coding technique for matrix and vector operations that reduces expensive rotation computations. Furthermore, SIMC 2.0 reduces the size of garbled circuits used for non-linear calculations and introduces an alternative lightweight protocol. As a result, our experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains for linear computations (up to 17.4 times faster), reduced computation and communication overhead in non-linear layers (by at least 1.3 times), and improved overall runtime by 2.3 to 4.3 times. SIMC 2.0's optimized design provides superior privacy preservation solutions with lower overhead, enabling reliable ML deployments even with poorly initialized bases. Our research includes a sensitive radio telescope observation of nearby spiral galaxy M101 and its surrounding region, conducted using the FAST. This allowed us to identify an enlarged and irregularly shaped HI disk around M101. Inside the optical disk of M101, the HI velocity field appears ordered, whereas there is a significant disturbance in the outer disk. In addition, three previously undetected HI clouds have been discovered near the southern edge of the M101 disk. These HI clouds have estimated masses of 1.3$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, 2.4$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$, and 2.0$\times$10$^{7}$ $M_{\odot}$ respectively. The HI clouds in M101 rotate in sync with its main HI disk. In contrast to a similar nearby galaxy, NGC 5477, which also shares a disk, these HI clouds in M101 have no visual counterparts. Also, a newly found HI tail in M101 supports evidence that the galaxy is interacting with its dwarf companion, NGC 5474. This interaction may be the origin of the extra-planar gas and HI tail observed in M101. In this study, various gas components and their relationships within M101 are further explored. The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other fundamental structures and fields. In this study, we introduce a direct procedure for dividing any element of a global domain (either a number domain or a global function domain) into the sum of the minimal-length squared components. This general domain includes algebraic number domains, algebraic function domains, and quadratic domains. The applicability of this approach also benefits other scenarios such as computing the norm of an irreducible factor of a polynomial equation in a global domain and determining the minimal value of a quadratic form over a global domain. Furthermore, this research leads to an unexpected discovery regarding the minimal number of components in the sum of squared components expression, which is shown to be in a linear relationship with the domain's global class number and a measure of the domain's global regulator. This finding provides an unprecedented, non-trivial field-based interpretation of the well-known Bourbaki conjecture concerning the minimal number of components in the sum of squared components expression, which we have recently shown to be correct. This was achieved through a previously unknown application of Grunzenhaber-Jordan development and a novel use of smooth representations of finite groups over global domains. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. As a result, this innovative approach has the potential to shift the paradigm in spectroscopy, making it an exciting development in the field. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on several graphs, including trees and more complex structures, and the effects of the graph connectivity and random walk strategy on performance are examined. The algorithm is also applied to a cancer treatment problem, involving the convergence of model estimates as the number of iterations increases. The advantages of the algorithm are further highlighted through a comparison with synthetic data. The associated code can be found here: https://github.com/ahmedossama20/FedRW. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  However, it is essential to conduct additional financial analysis to determine the exact return on investment.  A secondary finding shows that mental health treatment lowers the odds of recidivism regardless of the diagnosis but increases in impact when considering the type of diagnosis.  Future research should involve conducting a more in-depth financial analysis and an examination of why some offenders receive treatment while others do not.  It is also necessary to investigate potential court ordering patterns and their effect on the results.  In addition, it would be beneficial to conduct a longer-term analysis of the effect of mental health treatment on recidivism rates.  Finally, the data suggests that a model with offender-specific constants could better analyze the data than a model without such constants, indicating that there may be unobservable factors affecting an offender's likelihood of returning to the justice system.  Therefore, it is necessary to control for these individual factors when analyzing the effect of mental health treatment.  It is also possible that unobservable factors related to courts are influencing the results and, therefore, it is necessary to conduct more research on court ordering processes.  The data used for this analysis is based on convictions rather than arrests, which may lead to an accumulation of convictions for an individual but does not necessarily represent their total crime count.  Therefore, it would be beneficial to conduct a future analysis using arrest data. To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 12.8 gigabits per second during in-house and CERN integrated testing. With production scheduled for completion by the end of 2018, the full jFEX system will be ready for deployment before the LHC's anticipated 2021 restart. This will allow for the efficient detection of the Higgs boson in various decay channels, significantly expanding the possibilities for ATLAS's physics research beyond its current capabilities. This project has also paved the way for exploring the potential of jFEX's research in other particle detectors and scientific applications. This paper provides an in-depth overview of the jFEX system's design, its associated components, and the progress made to date, as well as offering insights into its future development and potential uses beyond its current LHC-based implementation. This paper also offers various jFEX-related design patterns that could be applied to other FPGAs and projects sharing similar processing and data transfer characteristics. By combining traditional rendering techniques with neural networks, Deferred Neural
Rendering achieves a balance between computational simplicity and visually realistic
images. Extending DNR to use skinned meshes for rendering dynamic objects would
significantly expand its potential applications. However, doing so requires accounting
for unmodeled mesh deformations and potential misalignments, which can otherwise
jeopardize the rendering pipeline. To address these challenges for realistic virtual
human avatars, we developed Articulated Neural Rendering, a new framework that
extends DNR. In experiments and user evaluations, ANR consistently outperformed not
only DNR but also other avatar creation methods, demonstrating its superiority
through clear preferences and outstanding results on quantitative assessment metrics.
ANR enabled significantly improved visual stability, level of detail, and overall
plausibility in both static and dynamic scenes. The significant enhancements
accompanied annotations from human operators with limited input, thereby reducing the
need for extensive training data. The code and models for ANR are openly available
at https://github.com/linguo/Articulated_Neural_Rendering. The examples can be
found at https://linguo.com/anr_experiments.html.

To gain a deeper understanding of the performance and lifespan of materials, 
it's crucial to assess their atomic disorder levels. To this end, we use a unique
approach that leverages graph neural networks to create an interpretable disorder 
metric, effectively capturing local atomic configuration variability across the
solid to liquid phase spectrum. This methodical approach is tested with three
models featuring different disorder levels, including interfaces between solid 
and liquid phases, multi-crystalline microstructures, and grain boundaries, 
using elemental aluminum as a prime example. Our study demonstrates how our 
approach tracks the space-time progression of interfaces and provides a precise 
definition of the boundary between order and disorder. Furthermore, we show 
how our disorder fields' physics-preserving gradients can be utilized to explain 
and predict the behavior and failure of materials. Overall, our framework serves 
as an accessible and universally applicable solution for analyzing the complex 
atomic structures within materials.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$, a function $\eta(\theta)$ and an unknown distribution $G$ as the mixing distribution. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The method is proven to be robust as it encompasses several popular estimation methods, such as Bayes estimation, providing the prior distribution is 'nice' and incorporating prior information is feasible. The approach to estimating $\eta_G$ is highly flexible and it is possible to derive the GMLE's properties on a case-by-case basis. The proposed method enables the derivation of asymptotic theory including the GMLE's root-n consistency under certain regularity conditions. The conditions are similar to those required for the consistency of regular maximum likelihood estimators. The work also explores the estimation of $\eta_G$ using GMLE's and we discuss how it relates to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under other loss functions. The results are demonstrated numerically on realistic examples and real data sets. The methods are supported by R package 'GMLE'. The package contains the most commonly used mixing distribution scenarios, including beta, Dirichlet, Gaussian and mixture distribution. The package also provides functions to generate theoretical results and diagnostic tools. The most recent version of the package can be found on the GitHub site. The site also contains the source files used to generate the results presented in the paper. The work is concluded by discussing potential future research directions, particularly the investigation of the proposed methods within context-based statistical theories. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. Our best model employing a modified alphabet achieved 29.6 WER%, whereas fine-tuning the model without alterations resulted in 33.5 WER%. Notably, our technique allowed us to achieve comparable ASR performance on Czech data with only minimal training on Czech, amounting to just 3.5 hours out of the 90 offered. Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data, specifically from quasi-two-body $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\pm}K^+K^-$ decays containing the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  The calculated distributions can be used to explain BaBar's measurements of the $B^+ \to K^+K^-K^-$ decay at an invariant mass $M(K^+K^-)\sim 1.5$ GeV, showing the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter. Additionally, we examine how this extra dimension affects the black hole dispersion velocity and find that it could be in line with velocity profiles observed in certain globular clusters. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot learning experiments. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our model has significant relevance, as studying it helps us comprehend the inner workings of sorting networks and its connections to the construction of recursive and efficient circuits for sorting. In particular, we aim to identify the lowest required comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with limited depth. Through our research, we found lower bounds on the comparator arity (k) for sorting networks with constant depth. Specifically, we found the smallest k that allows a sorting network with depth d = 1, 2, 3, or 4. We found that k is equal to n for d = 1 and 2. We also discovered that k is equal to n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3. Interestingly, we found that k is equal to n^2/3 when d = 4, indicating that it grows sublinearly in n. Notably, we found this sublinear behavior occurs earlier in sorting networks than in majority circuits, which require d = 3 to achieve k = n^2/3. We propose a new construction of a sorting network with k = n/2 (rounded up) for d = 3, which is an improvement over previous works. We also established that any sorting network with constant depth must have comparator arity (k) that grows linearly in n. Consequently, we conclude that the linearity threshold of sorting networks with constant depth occurs at k = n. Additionally, we explore the concept of identifying the minimum depth (d) required for sorting networks with binary comparators, which is an open question in the field. We propose a general method for constructing sorting networks with depth d + 1, which is applicable to any n that is a power of 2. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. A specific example is presented where an exact solution for a single-fluid star is given, and its anisotropic properties are verified. The non-uniform volume of a star is used to create an Eötvös parameter constraint, and in doing so, the existing upper limit on this parameter is narrowed. Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe that a bar forms in the center within one billion years, along with spiral arms composed of 2, 3, and 4-armed patterns. These features persist for at least 3 billion years in our simulations. However, we find that a bar won't develop if the galaxy's disk has a radial scale longer than 2.6 kiloparsecs. A compact bulge also prevents bar formation, as predicted. Our findings also indicate that a bar contributes to the maximum rotation curve in a galaxy's central regions due to its shape and orientation. Additionally, we predict that a bar will be observable in the Milky Way using stellar population diagrams, specifically in the 7 kiloparsecs radius range. Our model further suggests that star formation patterns within a galaxy's disk will be influenced by a bar. For example, a 4-armed spiral structure will transform into a 2-armed pattern when a bar forms in the center. Consequently, a compact bulge may indicate the presence of a bar in a galaxy like the Milky Way. Our study implies that a bar's potential energy accounts for up to 35% of a galaxy's stellar potential energy. Therefore, a bar should have a notable effect on the movements of stars within a galaxy's central regions. Lastly, we believe that a compact bulge may be the result of a bar's activity over time, specifically through the collision of a bar with the galaxy's central black hole. Our model also predicts that a bar will contribute to the influx of gas towards the galaxy's central regions, which in turn may increase the likelihood of a black hole's growth through feeding. Nevertheless, our simulation shows that a bar's formation doesn't significantly impact the galaxy's disk mass or bulge-to-halo mass ratio. Nevertheless, we find that a compact bulge which results from a bar's activity may increase the galaxy's disk mass by consuming gas in the center. Lastly, we believe that our findings have significant implications for the Milky Way's central regions, specifically in regards to its bulge and bar structure, which will be confirmable with future surveys such as the LSST, WFIRST, and VOSTRA. Lastly, we provide a framework for identifying the bar's presence, length, orientation, and potential impact on the galaxy's movements and star formation patterns. We also offer predictions on how this bar will influence the galaxy

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like shapes. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations, effectively impacting gas dynamics. A comparative analysis with existing simulations validates the realistic magnetic field model's effectiveness and provides greater insight into magnetic field influence on galaxy combinations. Ultimately, this study suggests that massive galaxy combinations with magnetic fields have a significant impact on magnetic field amplification, with potential to shape galaxy morphology in a way that differs from simulations without magnetic fields. The unique spiral and extended disc structures generated by these simulations present a challenge to further research and may serve as a model for understanding magnetic field influence on galaxy combinations. The realistic magnetic field model employed in this study will also be made available for public use.

To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The code and data are available at https://github/metagec.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating the impact of rounding errors to some extent. The theoretical insights are complemented by an investigation of the consequences of releasing population suicide rates with certain data characteristics. The theoretical findings are further validated through simulation studies. The methods discussed can be applied to address similar challenges in related areas. The corresponding software is also provided to facilitate the implementation of the proposed methods. The research was funded by the ISRF fellowship at the University of Geneva. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. This finding is expected to contribute significantly to a deeper understanding of the exotic ground state of GdInO3. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established a lower bound showing that for any mechanism with any number of agents, there exist situations in which all pure Nash equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations up to one good, thereby demonstrating the mechanistic benefit of using a round-robin allocation method with any number of agents. Our investigation advances our understanding of the interrelation between fair allocation and the existence of pure Nash equilibria, while also providing useful insights into the properties of established methods for achieving relaxed envy-free allocation in a non-selfish setting.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The code for our method has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/AlexeyOS/STA-UDA.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV. Furthermore, the ability to study individual rock crystals may allow for further enhancement by reducing contamination from radioactive background and enhancing the contrast between dark matter signals and cosmic radiation. Ultimately, paleo-detectors have the potential to offer a complementary approach to conventional dark matter detection methods, enabling the exploration of new parameter spaces despite unavoidable background limitations. This approach could provide a powerful tool for validating or disproving the existence of dark matter through a distinctive signature left in rocks across different time scales. Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled training data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in large-scale self-supervised image classification that utilize contrastive learning, we propose learning re-identification representations directly from large quantities of unlabeled surveillance video without relying on labels. By utilizing pre-trained pedestrian detection tools and applying contrastive loss at both the image and tracklet levels, we also integrate camera labels that are available free of charge for the principal component analysis step. Our large-scale evaluation of the method on an unlabeled dataset demonstrates significantly superior performance when compared to other methods that do not utilize training data from the target domain. Moreover, we observed a notable increase in accuracy with a larger dataset, thereby highlighting the method's immense potential as the dataset continues to expand in size and diversity. By making the code and model available on open-source platforms, we hope to accelerate the development of more advanced re-identification methods that can be applied to surveillance video. Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses. Nonetheless, we present the first public analysis employing the nested sampler and an extremely rigorous walk algorithm for sampling bias mitigation, along with a publicly accessible code for this specific analysis. This code allows users to conduct individual pulsar analyses and incorporate new datasets with ease. Moreover, we introduce the PTA4GNB package, which incorporates two methods for signal parameter estimation, as well as the batch processing of nested samplers for cross-validation and sampling bias evaluation. This code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyf116/PTA4GNB. We yield no significant signal parameter evidence but do identify sampling bias in approximately half of the datasets examined, a phenomenon that can be interpreted as noise or a manifestation of parameter degeneracy. This research lays the groundwork for future deep analyses and encourages the open sourcing of related code to facilitate collaborative research. Lastly, we provide the first derived low-resolution power density spectrum for five individual pulsars, which can be utilized in combination with other datasets in a global signal search. Moreover, we offer the opportunity for cross-validation and feedback on the code through the public GitHub repository.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. The implications of our study for the development of methods to compute the pion's form factor are also considered. This research is performed on an ensemble of configurations with gauge field configurations generated by the IFDPS collaboration using staggered fermions at their physical quark mass. The calculations are carried out on a $32^3 \times 64$ lattice space, allowing for an in-depth exploration of the pion's internal structure.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. Like participants in our study, people in general seem to underestimate the influence of luck on worker outcomes based on self-reported views, but overestimate its impact when actually seeing the data. This phenomenon could provide a partial explanation for the discrepancy between research on luck and inequality in the laboratory and in actual datasets. Finally, our study reveals that participants' opinions on reducing the income gap are less motivated by a desire to aid less fortunate individuals, when circumstances suggest that the gap is influenced by luck rather than poor decisions. This result is consistent with the idea that people distinguish between inequality caused by chance and those causes related to an individual's actions. It implies that the tendency to view the world as a meritocratic place, observed in the literature, may have implications for how people view the income gap. It suggests that people view income inequality resulting from luck as being less concerning in and of itself, which has further implications for how people view the income gap when circumstances suggest its extent is influenced by luck rather than poor decisions. It also implies that policies aimed at reducing income inequality due to luck should be distinguished from those aimed at reducing inequality resulting from poor decisions. It is only in the latter case that people exhibit a desire to aid those who are less fortunate. It has practical implications for how the impact of luck on worker outcomes is communicated to the public and how income inequality is framed in the debate. Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information to yield a coarser partial flag structure in $X'$. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. The computational frameworks, data sets, and software developed as part of this research are available for download at https://github.com/hungyiwang/datascope. The DataScope approach to computing the Shapley value for training examples paves the way for a broader understanding of the relationship between data quality and machine learning model performance. By establishing a threshold for radio signal intensity, we catalogued sources at the heart of the clusters and within areas surrounding the half of their brightness. Our statistical analysis indicated that there's a clear relationship between the density of radio signals in the cluster core and collision rates, mass, or their interaction at a 90% confidence level, yet we didn't observe a clear link between such factors and radio source counts within areas surrounding the half of their brightness. Some sources above our threshold intensity include millisecond pulsars, verified as well as black hole XRB candidates and unidentified others. Excluding the black holes from the analysis resulted in higher correlation significance at 99%, but excluding the collision rate alone, significantly lowered it to 68%. According to previous computer simulations about the collision dynamics within such clusters, their collision rate might not effectively forecast BH location, which supports our findings. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. The comprehensive studies of our approach's robustness and efficiency reveal that SIT offers a reliable and efficient way to learn from offline data, making it suitable for complex multi-agent scenarios. The code is available at: \url{https://github.com/huanghaoxian/SIT}. The paper is also publicly accessible at: \url{https://www.globalei.org/index.php/GEMM/article/view/637}.

In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, our analysis showcases the superiority of single-particle entanglement as a resource for quantum information processing, given its ability to execute non-local tasks involving vast distances, a capability absent in multi-particle entanglements. Single-particle entanglement should therefore be regarded as a distinct and superior resource in quantum information processing. The presented analysis counters objections posed by some researchers who have offered multi-particle entanglement as a substitute for single-particle entanglement, demonstrating that true non-locality in quantum mechanics emanates from single-particle entanglement. The presented proof also addresses the concern posed by Einstein in his 1927 speech, thereby validating the'spooky action at a distance' phenomenon. The validity of these conclusions is showcased via the Stern-Gerlach experiment, providing a clear and intuitive illustration of single-particle entanglement's genuine non-locality. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Barlett inequalities facilitate statistical analysis of codebook search performance. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our framework also enables the prediction of characteristics of nuclear star clusters and their Population III binary remnant contents that will be observable with future surveys and missions like the Square Kilometre Array and the Legacy Survey of Space and Solutions. Ultimately, our research suggests that nuclear star clusters are critical environments for Population III binary remnants and merit in-depth observational study in their own right. These observations have the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of the universe's earliest generations of stars. To ensure the performance of GECAM's Gamma-Ray Detectors (GRDs) and test its onboard triggering and localization software before launch, a portable device that simulates Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs) has been developed using a grid controlled X-ray tube and direct digital synthesis technologies. This portable GRB simulator, which modulates an X-ray flux powered by up to 20 kV, demonstrates its capability of generating high-energy bursts. Before its launch in December 2020, both GECAM satellites were tested using this simulator, which produced short and long GRBs that were detected and analyzed by the onboard GECAM/GRDs. The results showed a strong consistency between the observed data and the programmed simulation functions, indicating excellent performance of the GRDs and the GRB simulator. The simulator has since been launched alongside the GECAM satellites and is operating in orbit to provide in-flight calibration and testing of the GRDs. To further explore its capabilities, the simulator has generated multiple GRBs with varying characteristics, which were detected and analyzed by the GECAM/GRDs. The data collected has been used to conduct in-depth simulations of GRBs, including time and energy profiles, and the results have been compared with those from the Fermi Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor. The outcomes have provided valuable insights into the GRDs' performance and field calibration, and have demonstrated the simulator's ability to create complex cosmic events and generate useful on-board triggering and localization data even when it is operating independently. As the largest commercial X-ray flux modulator with the highest power, this simulator has a wide range of applications in various fields, including high-energy astrophysics, medical research, and industrial processing. As the base model of a future multi-band GRB detector is being developed, the simulator is being upgraded to generate more sophisticated bursts, such as weak and far-off-line triggers, and is being explored for its potential to generate other types of electromagnetic emissions resulting from gravitational waves. As the most advanced GRB simulator in the world, it is now ready to drive the development and operation of GECAM's GRDs and to contribute to the expansion of its scientific scope. This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2. These investigations are motivated by the recent breakthrough paper of P. Dukes and R. Zhao, further extending the family of BMOA-type spaces. Notably, our analysis provides the most comprehensive study on the semigroups of composition operators within the BMOA-type spaces context. Moreover, our results encompass both the classical BMOA case (p = 1) and the new family of VMOA_2, which is known as A^{\infty}. This research also offers a novel approach by establishing the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the compactness of the Volterra-type operators T_g on the BMOA-type spaces. These results are anticipated to contribute significance to the understanding of the semigroups of composition operators and their relationship with the compactness of the Volterra-type operators on the BMOA-type spaces. Additionally, our investigation of the compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2 is expected to provide valuable insights into the study of the maximal subspace of strong continuity. Moreover, our results on the semigroups of composition operators within the BMOA-type spaces context are anticipated to contribute to the broader family of F(p,q,s) spaces. Lastly, our investigation of the compactness of T_g on BMOA_2 is seen as an initial step to exploring the relationship between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the compactness of the Volterra-type operators T_g on more general BMOA-type spaces

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold. Furthermore, models simulating the progression of new knowledge reveal an N-shape, indicating that the most significant advancements occur during the accelerated phase. Ultimately, the findings suggest that the most valuable new knowledge is approximately 5-15 years old, depending on the discipline, and represents a crucial stage in the development of each area. Although this study focuses on the large-scale evolution of scientific knowledge, the proposed methodology can be applied to any time-series citation database. By providing a comprehensive framework for understanding the quantification of knowledge amount, the research offers a new perspective on the complex nature of scientific productivity. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the most valuable new knowledge is approximately 5-15 years old, representing a crucial stage in the development of each area, and merit consideration in funding prioritization. The associated dataset and code are available online.

The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for the development of secure, dual hop OFDM communication systems. Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can result from interactions with multiple edge modes within different energy gaps. Notably, we find that spontaneous emission from these sources can separate spatially, creating time-bin entangled states upon applying a single control pulse. Furthermore, we explore the possibility of emitters selectively interacting with distinct channels via light-matter coupling. These capabilities provide the foundation for implementing quantum operations among protected photons and generating complex, entangled states of light within these topological channels. Ultimately, this paves the way for realizing topologically protected quantum computations that harness the robust properties of these multi-mode waveguides. In addition, we discuss potential implementations using superconducting qubits and neutral atoms. Our study unveils the promise of combining quantum optics with topological phenomena in quantum electronics. In doing so, we identify the essential role emitters with controllable spontaneous emission play in achieving this vision. Lastly, we outline potential paths to overcoming the constraints imposed by spontaneous emission in complex light-matter interactions. In this context, we propose the utilization of emitters with selectively adjusted spontaneous emission properties. This capability could arise from the application of quantum phases, certain shapes of cavities, or specific parities in neutral atoms. In this manner, we can fully leverage the capabilities provided by robust quantum currents in topological physics. This represents a crucial step towards executing topologically protected quantum computations and a wide range of other optical operations. In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability. Additionally, we investigate how the system responds to diverse human driving styles and the connection between their predictive and adaptive components. We've also conducted experiments to demonstrate that the proposed method successfully prevents collisions and provides the highest possible level of passenger comfort. We've implemented this safety-oriented parking assistance system on a vehicle and successfully demonstrated its functionality at the 2019 International Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas. The associated software is now publicly accessible. Unlike existing parking assistance technologies that are intervention-based, our approach encourages a more cooperative relationship between human drivers and automated vehicles by utilizing variable message boards to disseminate important information. The system has already been adopted by multiple high-profile companies. Although our research focuses on parking, the same concepts can be applied to any situation involving automated vehicles waiting for traffic lights to change. The underlying idea revolves around the realization that the optimal waiting strategy for an automated vehicle is to maintain the same following distance as human drivers do in similar situations, providing a solid foundation for a predictive control system to generate safe pathways. The intricacies of this system include the incorporation of diverse human driving styles and their implications on the connection between predictive and adaptive components. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
As a result, researchers and the public can conduct and observe the same-level performances more quickly, which we've already done, obtaining new insights and revealing concerns with the current evaluation methodology. 
Matterially, we've observed a significant gap (around 200,000 actions per second) between simulated and actual interactions, a discrepancy that needs addressal to guarantee accuracy in comparative studies. 
Furthermore, we've discovered implicit biases in two of the three games, affecting the fairness of agent evaluations, which we've already taken steps to rectify. 
Alongside these advancements, we've introduced new evaluation metrics and methodologies, also available for public use, to better gauge the capabilities of virtual agents. 
These developments, incorporating results from initial trials of newly introduced agents, are now available for public access through our TextWorldExpress platform. 
It is essential for any proposed evaluation methods or results to undergo scrutiny by the research community through formal experimentation sessions, which we've established to ensure the integrity of the evaluation process. 
Ultimately, we're committed to continuous collaboration with researchers and the broader community to ensure the text-based game platform remains a trusted and reliable tool for assessing virtual agents. 
Alongside this paper, we're introducing a new website and set of documentation to provide easy access to TextWorldExpress, its evaluation methods, and associated data, also incorporating a guide for adding novel games to the platform. 
The source code for this paper is available under the MIT license on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ash8071/textworldexpress. 
The TextWorldExpress platform is now available at https://textworldexpress.github.io. 
The source code for the agent that produced the results discussed in this paper is available at https://github.com/ash8071/treasureagent. 
The text world models and evaluation metrics developed for this research have been contributed to the PyTorch repository.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the hardware accelerator exhibit high performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models by an order of magnitude in terms of model size while also demonstrating substantial improvements in accuracy across multiple video recognition datasets. Furthermore, the proposed FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to excel over a leading tensor decomposed hardware model called TIE in terms of throughput, area efficiency, and energy efficiency in various benchmark tests. As a consequence, this research leads to a major breakthrough in the development of hardware accelerators for LSTM-based video recognition models, making it feasible to apply this technology in actual applications. As a secondary outcome, the compact FDHT-LSTM models developed in this research also demonstrate superior performance to existing compressed LSTMs across multiple datasets. As a result, this research leads to a significant advancement in the field of LSTM-based video recognition and provides a model for further exploration of algorithm and hardware co-designs in deep learning applications. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. The associated code has been made publicly accessible.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The proposed conjecture of Charge Convexity, which encompasses not just the U(1) case, can be validated by testing the property of a convex spectrum of charges across a range of models where the dimensions of operators are analytically derivable through perturbation theory, expansions in N, and semi-classical approximations. Our exploratory examination reveals that the Charge Convexity Conjecture is upheld in each instance examined, yet we have not discerned the underlying reason for this behavior from the perspective of conformal field theory. On the other hand, within anti-de Sitter space, the relationship involving the dimension of an operator and its charge can be re-expressed through the mass and charge of a particle of minimal width, thereby confirming the Weak Gravity Conjecture in this specific context. The extension of our investigation to new scenarios, such as theories with global symmetries that are not gauge symmetries, theories with a high number of gauge symmetries, such as SU(N) gauge theories, along with a separate examination of the relationship involving the dimension of an operator, and its charge under a global symmetry that is not gauge symmetry, have been included in the study. The findings from our exploratory examination reveal that the property of a convex spectrum of charges is upheld in each instance examined. The scope of our investigation also discloses that the property of a convex spectrum of charges applies broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary, thereby validating the conjecture of Charge Convexity.
