Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Moreover, the proposed method achieves enhanced denoising performance, especially in simulating high-dose images from low-dose images, and can be a valuable tool for widening the application range of low-dose CT imaging. Additionally, we have introduced a new cycleGAN training configuration that can be useful for other image enhancement tasks. The proposed algorithm has been implemented and is available for public use on GitHub, along with sample codes on Tencent AI Cloud. The corresponding authors can be reached on email for further details. The quantitative and qualitative evaluation of our new cycleGAN approach validate its efficacy. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. Our research is a significant step towards developing efficient video super-resolution models, with future directions discussed in the conclusion section. Our code and model have been made available on MMEditing.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. The available code and studies within this research are accessible at the referenced repository.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Code is available at: https://github.com/owenscase/mfmbf-mrl.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. We further establish connections to other fundamental theoretical limits, notably Herbrand's Theorem from 1930, the Undecidability of Arithmetics proven by Godel in 1931, and the implications of the Theorems of Anselm and Cantor. We then explore the pivotal role these theorems and their common proof basis play in the creative aspects of mathematics within the context of cognitive science and the philosophy of mathematics. We offer an novel perspective on the relationship between these ground-breaking results and the fundamental components of mathematics, specifically the interplay between formal systems, reasoning, and the fundamental axioms and theorems within these systems. We contend that this perspective provides a suitable foundation for a pedagogical approach that places these theorems at the forefront of introductory courses on the limits of mathematical knowledge and the foundations of mathematics. We support this approach through proposed modifications to standard course curricula and are supported by exemplary chapters for potential textbook inclusions. Ultimately, we aim to inspire a greater emphasis on highlighting the creative aspects of mathematics within the broader context of cognitive science and philosophy within mathematics education. We also provide a potential framework for a graduate level course centered on these concepts and are eager for feedback from the academic community. We further outline potential collaborations and research opportunities driven by this approach and are eager for like-minded academics to join in this endeavor. We conclude by emphasizing the significance of making the incredible human achievements behind these ground-breaking results accessible to a broader audience and the potential for this perspective to shape the future of mathematics education and beyond. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. The new theorem enables the identification of a significant range, denoted as Δ_{R_1, R_2, R_3}, within the right half-plane of the complex λ-plane. Within this range, any function u, satisfying the equation Δ^2u = λu, cannot vanish on three distinct circles while remaining non-zero throughout the first circle. Furthermore, we establish that the lower bound for the smallest eigenvalue λ may be determined as greater than -1/R^2, where R is the smallest distance between two of the circles. This breakthrough is achieved through the introduction of a monogenic analogue of the Schuster package, allowing the application of techniques employed in the proof of Hadamard's theorem. Additionally, this development facilitates future investigations of theorems for multiple functions satisfying the same conditions. It is also demonstrated that theorems of this nature may be related to boundary value problems in the space R^n+1. As such, these breakthroughs provide valuable insights for further research within the field of Clifford analysis. As a notable aspect, the approach takes into account the unique characteristics of the M-valued hyperanalytic functions. The paper also introduces an innovative method for estimating the lower bound for the smallest eigenvalue λ. This method may also be applied to non-circular shapes, such as polygons, by employing the technique of homotopy. When the population is not fully known in advance, sampling occurs in sequence, either individually or in batches, which are obtained sequentially. This work presents a novel algorithm that allows for sequential selection of a balanced sample. The algorithm accommodates equal and unequal inclusion probabilities and can also be applied to select spatially balanced samples when the population contains geographical coordinates. Moreover, an investigation using simulated data reveals that the proposed method surpasses alternative methods. Additionally, the method is validated using real-world data and compared to other methods. The software that implements the algorithm is part of the 'Spatial' package available in R. Alongside the algorithm, other methods for sequential selection are also investigated; however, it is evident that they do not effectively promote the inclusion of diverse units. Conversely, the proposed method successfully achieves this goal. The benefits of the method are also reflected in reduced sampling costs without compromising diversity. The method's performance is investigated in relation to the design of class subpopulations and it is observed that it is particularly useful when sampling from large populations. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Ultimately, despite the exceptional performance of direct prediction in our tests, its efficacy may depend heavily on the data used and therefore further research is required to validate these findings across different real-world training datasets. The exceptional outcome from the direct prediction approach, however, did raise questions about the potential for similar AI-based methods to succeed in this task despite relying on simplified training processes. As a result of this research, we are contributing the trained models and related code to the community in the hope of sparking further discussion and investigation in this area. As part of this contribution, we are also sharing the simulated dataset that was used to train the models, along with related code to train the camera pose estimation models, making it easier for others to reproduce our results and explore new directions. The code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/ultracoder3/camera-pose-estimation-barriers. As the field of artificial intelligence continues to evolve at a rapid pace, it is becoming increasingly essential to re-evaluate established facts about the field through rigorous testing and validation. As a part of this research, we are contributing the results from our investigation into the camera pose estimation barrier we had previously identified, which stated that deep learning models could not successfully estimate camera poses directly from images. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Our approach demonstrates the potential to solve complex inverse problems by leveraging deep neural network architecture. Additionally, it addresses a common issue of inverse problems - the lack of measurable output - by providing a way to generate meaningful samples directly from the solution, given the prior distribution. We showed that our approach overcomes limitations of the original GAN model by providing a way to control the generation process and integrate prior knowledge. The code for the proposed method and evaluation scripts have been made available online at https://github.com/yunsongliu/ccwgan. The paper's results have also been posted online at https://yunsongliu.github.io/project/ccwgan. The paper has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. We conclude by discussing the crucial role that invariant manifolds play in the analysis of the behavior of dynamical systems. We also provide examples illustrating the application of these conditions to various systems. Lastly, we outline the potential for extension of these conditions to a broader framework applicable to a greater range of dynamical systems. This line of inquiry may lead to a deeper understanding of how the invariant manifolds facilitate the analysis of the system's activity along those manifolds. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications because THz signals face high absorption in the atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, researchers have explored the potential of multi-hop directional transmission techniques to extend communication range, albeit these schemes can result in prolonged beam training time using conventional methods such as exhaustive search or hierarchical approaches. To tackle this problem, a novel hierarchical beam training technique is proposed in this paper that dynamically optimizes training levels across individual single-hop links, maximizing overall spectral efficiency. To tackle this optimization problem in the presence of channel state uncertainty and noise, a reinforcement learning solution inspired by the multi-armed bandit problem is proposed. Simulations show the new technique converges quickly in dynamic channel conditions and offers up to 75% better performance than conventional methods in terms of spectral efficiency. The proposed method is also analyzed through practical multi-hop communications simulations, yielding results comparable to theoretically optimal performance with minimal beam training overhead. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Contrastingly, the other five screens occupy regions of dense gas and star formation, such as the Taurus Molecular Cloud and the Lambda Persei association. The spin periods of two scintillation screens match those of nearby A-type stars, suggesting a possible connection between the screens and the stellar activity. Furthermore, the orientation of one screen mirrors that of the nearby pulsar PSR B1111+01, suggesting a possible alignment related to the magnetic field. The screen associated with the void within the Local Bubble exhibits characteristics that differ from the others, including a much faster velocity and eccentric orbit. The findings of this research offer a comprehensive insight into the screens' properties and their connection to the surrounding environment, contributing to a better understanding of the complex relationships between the interstellar medium and its components. The discovered screens provide a reference point for comparing screens in the future, offering a chance to monitor the changes in the interstellar medium over time. Moreover, they pave the way for analyzing screens in relation to other celestial objects and studying the microstructure of the interstellar medium. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Additionally, subjective assessments confirm that QPNet can improve both internal speaker and text-to-speech applications. The source code is available online at https://github.com/yunsong-ai/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet.

This research presents a novel annotation and correction tool for Arabic texts,
namely MADARi, catering to Standard and Dialectal varieties. MADARi offers a user-
friendly interface and efficient management capabilities for annotating and handling
a considerable volume of texts. Its key features encompass a range of morphological
annotations, such as identifying the base form of words, associated clitics, part of
speech, lemma, translation, and dialect-specific markers. To facilitate productivity,
MADARi offers a set of built-in tools, including precomputed analysis to guide
annotators, access to multiple dialects via morphological analyzers, and retrieval
of prior annotations. Additionally, MADARi enables lead annotators to supervise and
coordinate the annotation process in a distributed and concurrent manner. We delve
into the rationale, design, and execution of this interface and present results from
an experiment conducted with the system. We also examine the efficacy of mediator-
less annotation, namely the impact of prior annotations on subsequent annotators.
Finally, we share our team's participation in the SuperZero out-of-domain dialect
identification task, showcasing the potential of dialect annotation. MADARi is now
available online at the specified URL.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Moreover, this relationship enables the derivation of shadows for bicategories obtained through Morita equivalence, essentially providing a way to compute the shadows of a bicategory without having access to its underlying THH. This calculation can be particularly useful when working with bicategories whose THH cannot be directly computed, such as certain bicategories associated with topological category theories like K-theory and functors between them. Ultimately, this framework offers a new perspective on the relationship between shadows and THH of bicategories, its applications including the derivation of shadows for bicategories of algebras over operads and its connection to rationalization in homotopy theory. This work is a part of a broader project that explores the relationship between bicategorical THHH and shadows, its ultimate goal being to establish the connection between the former and homotopy algebraic $K$-theory. This purpose underlies the development of new computational tools for calculating shadows, coupled with an intuitive presentation of fundamental concepts within the theory through publicly accessible code. This code not only facilitates the calculation of shadows for sample bicategories but also serves as a starting point for further research in this field. This research is supported by a grant from the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research, and the authors are also supported by NSERC and a CIFAR fellowship. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. All code and model weights are available for download at https://github.com/hjdw/ISCL. The VGG-Sound Source dataset has been uploaded to the VGG Image Grounding Website.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Moreover, LGCN showcases improved robustness against noisy edges and outperforms existing methods on unsupervised classification tasks. The source code of LGCN is available online. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Additionally, a single 3D computational example showcases the effectiveness of a sparse surface measurement procedure. These findings indicate that only limited observations of the boundary values can yield unique information about the source term within the interior of the domain. A parallel discussion on the issue of uniqueness in the absence of damping is also presented. The source term's recoverability through sparse observations has implications for the development of more efficient control strategies in such acoustic structures. The associated numerical approach employs a combination of the boundary control method and the sparse surface measurement procedure, as demonstrated through a simulation involving a flexible plate surrounded by air. The results highlight the ability to recover the source term by controlling the plate's vibrations at a small number of sparse locations, as shown in the accompanying video. The implications of these findings for future research on the sparse surface measurement procedure are also considered. variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our exponential delay discounting
model is a special case of the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting model, and
discuss its applications and limitations. Additionally, we include a dataset of
college students from the USA, China and Brazil, and employ orthogonality
priors for our Bayesian analysis of the data. By comparing different delay
discounting models, we find that the Tsallis distribution provides the best fit. 
We also identify factors influencing standard deviations of impulsivity, including
gender and country of origin, but not income. Lastly, we explore the structural
components of impulsivity by conducting a factor analysis, and discover that
average impulsivity is distinct from standard deviation in various tasks and
contexts. Our findings highlight the significance of considering the diversity
of impulsivity in scientific investigations, and suggest that the Tsallis delay
discounting model is a valuable tool for analyzing delay discounting data. 
However, our results should be interpreted with caution due to the limited
size of the dataset used. 
We propose that future research be conducted with a more substantial and
more diverse dataset, including older adults, to further examine the Tsallis
delay discounting model.

Furthermore, we suggest a novel experimental approach utilizing coherent light as an alternative method for determining negative temperature conditions. This proposal is applicable to any system with energy levels spanning a continuous spectrum, such as gas-phase polyatomic molecules. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to personalize patient treatment and follow-up, ultimately reducing the risk of undetected invasive carcinomas. The process of polyp characterization involves examining tissue samples for malignancy and dysplasia using histological analysis. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved medical pattern recognition accuracy; however, training these models necessitates vast collections of annotated medical images. In this context, we've developed UniToPatho, an extensive dataset consisting of 9536 annotated H&E stained patches derived from 292 whole-slide images, designed for deep learning-based classification and grading of colorectal polyps and adenomas. This dataset serves as a resource for researchers tackling the complex task of automating colorectal polyp characterization. Notably, it differs from other available datasets in several key ways, as it includes a broader range of grades, more comprehensive spectral variability, and specific annotations for carcinoma, high-grade and low-grade dysplasia, and adenomas. We've also conducted various experiments utilizing UniToPatho in conjunction with other datasets, demonstrating the potential of deep learning models in classifying and grading colorectal polyps and adenomas. The code and dataset are available at this link: https://github.com/laic95/UniToPatho. The dataset itself can be accessed via the following link: https://zenodo.org/record/5079282. The characters used in the dataset are in accordance with the Whole-Slide Image Analysis (WSI) community standards, and we've also included the code for a recent advanced model. This code, along with additional model architectures, is provided with the aim of advancing the field and encouraging further research in this area. The UniToPatho dataset represents a significant step towards creating a comprehensive collection of annotated images for colorectal polyps and adenomas, and we hope it will contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable deep learning models capable of characterizing colorectal polyps with certainty in an uncontrolled domain. The current benchmark achieves a classification accuracy of 85% and a F1-score of 83% for grading, and we believe a reliable model capable of distinguishing carcinoma from non-neoplastic tissue has yet to be developed. Therefore, we're offering a new challenge within the UniToPatho dataset, specifically focused on detecting carcinoma, and we look forward to seeing the progress made by researchers in this area. A novel numerical approach has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach operates within a time-domain framework, consisting of three main components: generating a suitable incoming plane wave with compact propagation direction, solving the time-domain scattering problem, and ultimately deriving the time-harmonic solution via Fourier transformation. Crucial to this approach is a dynamic front-tracking mesh adaptation technique which minimizes the required computational degrees of freedom, thereby enhancing performance by limiting support to the wave front's spatial extent. To complement this strategy, an alternative Fourier transformation method is developed, taking advantage of the optimized mesh dimensions for even better results. Successful applications and examples highlight the method's efficiency and adaptability with various sources, including external points and soft-scattering scenarios. However, it should be noted that trapping modes significantly reduce the method's efficiency. As such, further research is needed to address this limitation. The introduced approach is complemented by a comprehensive Fourier transformation method, leveraging the optimized mesh dimensions to yield precise time-harmonic solutions. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water content in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. In contrast to the water-rich Antarctic samples with terrestrial contamination, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals showed lower levels of water (around 0.018-0.087 wt.$\%$ H$_2$O) and D-poor isotopic signatures, ranging from -444 to -49. Evaluating various processes on small parent bodies, our analysis suggested minimal water loss during thermal metamorphism, and the water content in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals can be explained by a mixture of D-poor nebular hydrogen and D-rich water from mesostases. Approximately 45-95$\%$ of water with low D isotope values in the pyroxene minerals came from nebular hydrogen, and it's possible that S-type asteroids with nominally anhydrous minerals can hold significant amounts of water (254-518 ppm). This finding may imply a reduced need for additional volatile delivery to the terrestrial planets during the final stages of planetary accretion, given the water added to the nominally dry inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process. 

Furthermore, we discovered a positive correlation between water content and the $^{17}$O abundance in pyroxene minerals from the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk chondrites, which can be attributed to the addition of water with enriched $^{17}$O abundance from mesostases. This $^{17}$O enriched water may have originated from the incorporation of iron-rich olivine grains that went through thermal metamorphism on the parent bodies, resulting in the release of $^{17}$O enriched water from these grains. 

In addition, our analysis of Antarctic chondrite finds revealed a diverse range of hydrogen isotopic compositions and water content, which can be attributed to the effects of terrestrial contamination and varying degrees of thermal metamorphism. Nonetheless, it's possible that the water added to the inner Solar System bodies during the accretion process could also be responsible for the overall low D-poor isotopic signatures observed in the Benenitra and Chelyabinsk pyroxene minerals. This could provide a significant amount of water with low D isotope values for the terrestrial planets to consume during their formation, reducing the need for additional volatile delivery.

Using the algebraic Bethe-ansatz method, we find exact expressions for scalar products and form factors of higher-spin XXZ chains. This applies to any spin values and mixtures thereof. We verify the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the XXZ chain's monodromy matrix, enabling exact derivation. Specifically, we use quantum-group symmetry to explicitly obtain diagonalized forms for the B and C operators within the F-basis of the spin-1/2 XXZ chain. This achievement substantiates prior conjectures about the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations. These results provide a crucial foundation for systematic studies of form factors and correlation functions across solvable models connected to integrable XXZ spin chains. Moreover, they pave the way for a deeper understanding of the spin-chain's quantum-group symmetry, embedded as a irreducible representation within the algebra of scattering states. This development is evident when considering the quantum-group-symmetry-based algebraic Bethe-ansatz for the XXZ chain, introduced in our companion paper. This new approach enables direct computation of excited states and form factors without necessity for prior knowledge of the Lax operator's fusion basis. This breakthrough results from a combination of the affine quantum-group symmetry and the B and C operators' explicit forms, explicitly obtained here for the spin-1/2 XXZ chain, labeled as the $N=2$ ADE chain. This achievement provides a long-sought foundation for a systematic exploration of the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's correlation function calculations, also extending to models connected to the XXZ chain through integrable chains. This development is equally applicable to the spin-1/2 Heisenberg ferromagnetic chain, a well-known analogue of the XXZ chain. This situation arises because the XXZ chain shares the same algebraic structure with the Heisenberg chain, ensured by appropriate rescaling of the coupling constant. This shared algebraic structure ensures the affine quantum-group symmetry, $U_q(\hat{sl_2})$, for the Heisenberg chain's monodromy matrix, allowing our results to also apply directly to the Heisenberg chain. This shared algebraic structure further guarantees the algebraic Bethe-ansatz's applicability to the Heisenberg chain, also encompassing its correlation functions and scattering states. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language across different tongues. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. Additionally, our experiments demonstrate enhanced performance in domains with limited data availability and for more distant language pairs. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles composed of semiconductors, dielectrics, and metals over a broad range of wavelengths spanning from the dipolar regime down to the Mie regime. Our model reveals an unanticipated discrepancy in force components proportional to the square of the particle size for semiconductor particles, which cannot be explained by the scattering behavior alone. This discrepancy may be related to the intrinsic properties of the material. Furthermore, our model highlights the importance of considering temperature-induced effects on the multipoles, especially for semiconductor particles at room temperature. Our results indicate that these multipoles can provide a useful framework for comparing the electromagnetic scattering properties of different materials and understanding the underlying mechanisms governing optical force and thermal effects in microscale systems. Consequently, this approach may offer a useful pathway for investigating heat-induced effects in optical systems, in addition to providing greater flexibility in modeling the optical force, particularly when incorporating quantum effects, such as in superconducting devices. Ultimately, this multipoles-based model may provide a useful platform for tackling more intricate problems involving the interplay between light, matter, and heat at the microscale. This level of description can also support the development of light-matter systems with tunable interactions and could potentially enable the design of new quantum devices that can manipulate both the optical force and thermal effects, thereby providing a degree of freedom to control the interplay between light, matter, and heat at the microscale. This study introduces two categories of elements in the algebra U(gl(n)), specifically double Young-Capelli bitableaux and central Schur elements, both displaying remarkable action on the highest weight vectors of irreducible Schur modules. The central Schur elements can be viewed as a sum of double Young-Capelli bitableaux corresponding to various strictly increasing Young tableaux. These elements equate to preimages under the Harish-Chandra isomorphism of shifted Schur polynomials, aligning with quantum immanants as per Okounkov. Notably, the representation of Schur elements/quantum immanants bypasses reliance on irreducible characters of symmetric groups. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Moreover, we investigate the likelihood of observing the predicted radiative "solar" scale in future experiments, such as T2K and CLFASii. The simplest scoto-seesaw model offers promising explanations for several phenomena with independent origins. These include the dark matter composition in the Galactic Center and the binding energy of the Milky Way's halo, in addition to the matter-dominated cosmological evolution. The model also provides a novel framework for the implementation of the axion dark matter within the context of the "missing partner" type-I seesaw theory. The axion's radiatively induced coupling with the neutrino "solar" scale may be validated or contradicted in the near future. The simplest scoto-seesaw model offers a coherent framework that addresses the issues of neutrino, dark matter, and dark energy, making it a viable candidate for a theory beyond the Standard Model. This could potentially be verified or disproved in the next generation of particle and astrophysical experiments. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. The developed framework is also applicable to other $d$-shell systems displaying analogous orbital structure. The calculated parameters are tabulated for all 4d and 5d transition metal oxides, providing a necessary correction to previously published models and offering a more accurate foundation for future theoretical studies of transition metal oxides. The parameters are further illustrated through the example of GdNiO$_3$, where $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing is analyzed in detail and its consequences for orbital occupation and magnetic moment evaluated. The importance of intermediate electron-electron coupling in transition metal oxides is emphasized by considering the related issue of spin exchange and orbital occupation in Cu$^{+}$ impurities within these materials. The derived parameters hold the potential to significantly impact our understanding of the physics governing these materials and systems, also enriching the discussion on the nature of exchange coupling in these materials. The developed approach is anticipated to facilitate a more accurate interpretation of experimental data and a greater insight into the underlying physics of transition metal oxides and related systems. The framework is proposed for adoption in future first-principles simulations of magnetic properties in these materials. The calculated parameters are made publicly accessible to foster a greater collaboration and discussion within the scientific community. The findings are expected to stimulate a fresh evaluation of experimental branching ratios and magnetic properties in transition metal oxides, as well as the development of new theoretical models for these materials. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. The code used for these experiments is also included in this paper as an example of how to implement the algorithm efficiently in MATLAB. The algorithm has potential applications in various other problems, such as electrostatics and gravitational interactions. The algorithm is particularly useful for solving time-dependent and nonlinear equations, and it can also be adapted for use in finite volume methods. The algorithm is now available on MATLAB File Exchange under the name 'NewtonianPotential'.
